maintopic: NUCLEAR TEST EXPLOSION IN ALBERTA TAR SANDS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: NUCLEAR TEST EXPLOSION IN ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister, of which I have sent him notice. Would the Prime Minister care to comment on the article appearing on the front page of the Montreal Gazette of this morning headed "A-Blast Set for Alberta Oil Sands"?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: NUCLEAR TEST EXPLOSION IN ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext:
I have read the article in question, and without going into details respecting the same I wish to say that any decision as to whether a nuclear test explosion will be made in Canada in connection with the Alberta tar sands depends entirely on the government of Canada, and is not a question which the United States atomic energy commission can decide.
There has been no decision to authorize a nuclear test explosion in the tar sands area. Indeed, under the regulations made under the provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act no one can deal in any way with fissionable substances in Canada except by permission of the atomic energy control board of Canada. That board has not received any application from the United States atomic energy commission or any other person or persons for permission to carry out any explosion of a nuclear device in these sands.
That is as far as I want to go on this occasion, again underlining the fact that the government of Canada has not decided to authorize a nuclear test explosion and that no application has been made, and therefore the article in question is not borne out by the facts.

maintopic: NUCLEAR TEST EXPLOSION IN ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this question I wonder if the Prime Minister could say whether any discussions are taking place or whether any inquiries are being made within any of the departments as to the feasibility of such a test? I would also ask the Prime Minister, if any such studies are under way, whether these would be called off while negotiations for the cessation of nuclear weapons tests are going on so favourably.

Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: NUCLEAR TEST EXPLOSION IN ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that the hon. gentleman asks the question indicates that he knows the answer, which is that there have been discussions going on among various departmental officials relative to the technical basis for action along the line indicated. However, in so far as the government is concerned its view has been expressed on previous occasions, that it is opposed to tests. In so far as tests are concerned which would be for the good of mankind, I mentioned the other day the attitude that had been taken some two years ago by myself, speaking for the government.
In saying that, however, I want to make it clear that in my opinion so long as these disarmament discussions are continuing, any kind of nuclear test should certainly not be considered.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: NUCLEAR TEST EXPLOSION IN ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the Prime Minister's statement that the government is opposed to tests, and his reference to his statement of two years ago on this subject, may I ask him whether the statement he has just made modifies the statement made on that earlier occasion, August 22, 1958, as reported at page 3944 of Hansard, to this effect:
-on several occasions since I became Prime Minister I have advocated the suspension of nuclear tests, but always providing there was adequate international control to ensure the observance of the undertakings made in that connection.

maintopic: NUCLEAR TEST EXPLOSION IN ALBERTA TAR SANDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in so far as this earlier statement is concerned, there have been developments since then. I see no contradiction in the viewpoint expressed today and that expressed two years ago, except that naturally with the events that are now taking place modifications become necessary in order to meet changing conditions. Possibly what 1 have said should not be considered as a modification. What it is in fact is an interpretation of an actual reality existing today.

maintopic: REPORTED U.S. SUPPORT OF COMMON MARKET GROUP

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED U.S. SUPPORT OF COMMON MARKET GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I apologize for not sending him notice but I just spotted the article as the bell was ringing. My question is based on a press dispatch from Washington dated March 20 and entitled, "Inner Six Gets Support of United States in Trade Row", which reads in part as follows:
The United States has quietly come to the support of the European common market against the rival free trade association.

By backing the latest manoeuvre of the six-nation common market in a new and bitter phase of the European trade dispute, the United States has caused distress and even anger among members of the seven-nation European free trade association, led by Britain.
In view of statements by the government that we were marching in step with Britain and the United States in trade matters, would the minister be able to tell the house in which direction the government will be marching now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. SUPPORT OF COMMON MARKET GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am at some disadvantage in not having seen the article which has so suddenly come to the attention of the hon. member, but the organization of the Six and of the Seven is very well known to everyone. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and I participated in the conference at Paris in January with regard to this particular problem, where we were able to suggest a compromise in the apparent dispute between the Six and the Seven on that occasion.
I think there is nothing disturbing with regard to present developments and that we shall find ourselves marching in step with all countries that are interested in extending their trade, which is precisely what the Six and the Seven are interested in doing.
The article suggests that there is some conflict between the United States and Great Britain with regard to those regional trading blocs in Europe. That was not obvious to us at the conference at Paris.

speechtext: Order. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Then, Mr. Speaker, I would like to rise on a question of privilege and bring to your attention the fact that on Friday, when the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) brought this matter before the house and I did bring up a question of privilege, Your Honour seemed at that time to agree with me that it was a matter of privilege; and, since some of those hon. members are now in the house, I think it is a question of privilege to determine, at least in so far as the government is concerned, whether the house is going to be entitled to receive information of this character, or whether it is going to be given outside the house.
In the statements which the hon. member for Essex East brought to Your Honour's attention on Friday, there was a statement by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean) in which he said he understood that the federal government planned to propose legislation limiting hanging to certain types of murder. To that I would like to add the statement made in Hamilton by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney) on March 1, and one made by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) as reported in the Ottawa Journal on the same day. Both are of the same nature. I think perhaps I should put them on the record, because this is the matter of privilege.
Frank McGee. Toronto-Scarborough Progressive Conservative, told the North York Progressive Conservative association last night:
"I think it will come to a vote now but I can't see it passing".
He was referring to the capital punishment bill before the house. I continue:
He said the next move likely would be a compromise bill sponsored by the government which likely would reduce the number of offences for which the death penalty is the ultimate sentence.
Arthur Maloney, Conservative, Toronto Parkdale, who spoke in the commons in favour of abolition of capital punishment for murder, said in Hamilton last night that he expected the abolition bill to be defeated and be followed by government legislation
Inquiries of the Ministry
taking into account the views expressed in the debate. Mr. Maloney's comment supported a growing opinion on parliament hill that, whether the abolition bill is defeated in a vote or talked out, the government intends to take action to revise the law.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT

I understand that one and perhaps two of the hon. members who made such statements are here, and what I am complaining about is that surely the government should find it possible to tell us here in the house what its plans are in connection with this matter at a time when three members, in breach of privilege, I respectfully submit, have indicated outside of the house-

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: -what the government intends to do.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the Leader of the Opposition asked whether there was anything to report about the date of the forthcoming commonwealth prime ministers'

Inquiries of the Ministry conference, which date has appeared in the press, or the items which might be discussed at that conference, reports of which have also appeared in the press.
In so far as the first matter is concerned, I refer the Leader of the Opposition to a press release issued on December 15, 1959, in which it was stated that the commonwealth prime ministers' conference would begin in London on May 3. Since then it has been determined as well that the conference will close on May 13.
So far as the agenda of the conference is concerned, the hon. gentleman knows from his experience that it is not the practice to make public the agenda for the conference. It is true that from time to time there are speculative articles on the agenda, but because of the agreed and established practice of not disclosing the agenda, press speculation is not made the subject of official comment. The latest declaration in this regard was made in the British House of Commons on December 15, 1959, at which time Prime Minister Macmillan replied in like manner to questions then being asked respecting the matters which will come before this conference.
As the hon. gentleman knows, the field of commonwealth and international matters is generally traversed. Beyond that, the experience of the past has been that no fixed agenda is followed, and that each and every prime minister, having equal status in the conference, may bring before the conference such matters as in his opinion deserve to be considered.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of the very low grain quotas still in existence at many marketing points, particularly in southern Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Can the minister indicate what action he is considering to remove this gross discrimination and unfairness?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Assiniboia, I think, raised the same question two or three weeks ago. I protested then against the use of the word "discrimination", and today he has added the words "gross unfairness".
As everybody out west knows, and as the hon. member for Assiniboia knows only too well, the wheat board was faced with a very difficult situation during the fall and winter


months in moving large quantities of damp grain to the terminal elevators where that grain could be dried. In order to accomplish this, it meant that farmers living in other parts of the prairie provinces whose grain had not suffered would have to wait for a period before the quotas in their areas could be raised.
This situation was well known and was mentioned in the house in January. At the present time every effort is being made to stimulate the movement of dry grain from the areas that have been waiting so long, and hundreds of box cars are moving out west to pick up that grain from the country elevators. The quota allotment will be raised very quickly in some of the areas that have been on small quotas, and before much time has elapsed I think there will be a close equalization of quota distribution across the country. The causes for the present distinction between one area and another were simply weather conditions last fall, as all the farmers are well aware.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask the minister a supplementary question. Does the minister not feel that a substantial part of this very difficult situation arises from the fact that total marketings were 40 million bushels less than at this time about a year ago, and would the minister say whether or not he expects that some of this discrimination could be removed as a result of-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: Order. The hon. member's question is a bit leading and seems to be more in the nature of a statement than a request for information. He repeats the charge of discrimination, which is an improper tag to put on a question. I ask whether this question is not actually the substance of the motion which is to be referred in the house for consideration by a committee to deal with the delivery of grain by producers-

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: No. On the point of order which you have raised, Mr. Speaker, I may say that is an entirely different situation, one of marketing within the local area to a feed mill a few miles away from where the grain is produced. The other question relates to the tremendous marketings that ordinarily go for export.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: I thought the matter might be properly left over until it came before the committee. However, if the hon. member wishes information and will frame his question in a proper manner, I will admit it.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
1 am not trying to use the word "discrimination" if some other word is more appropriate, such as "unfair" or "unequal". I do not know how to describe it. However,

I ask the minister whether some of this unfairness, if he cares for that word, has arisen because total marketings have been less and not just because of the damp grain. Could the minister hold out any hope to grain producers that there may be some improvement this year over last year, considering the low quantities of grain that moved through the seaway?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I accept the word "inequality", rather than "discrimination" or "unfairness". The total marketings out west-

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: That is because you are on that side of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: -that is the deliveries by the farmers to the country elevators, have been delayed this year because of the conditions I have already mentioned. Actually the overseas clearances of wheat have been running ahead of last year and are still ahead of last year by between 3 million and 4 million bushels, so there has been no delay or restriction in the overseas movements, and that is reflected back to the market throughout the prairie provinces.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: I wonder whether the minister would answer my question, which was, does the minister feel there could be an improvement in the shipment of grain through the St. Lawrence seaway, which had fallen so drastically last summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: The course of events will indicate that. It depends on the orders which are placed for shipment through the seaway. If the orders are placed at the port of Churchill or at Vancouver, as so frequently happens, that is where the shipment is made; but much depends on the activity of the trade in general.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext:
May I
ask a supplementary question. Would the minister agree that one of the necessary results of taking the tough and damp grain to the terminal elevators, which has always seemed a perfectly proper and normal course, has been that the other grain was not in position in Vancouver to be loaded on the waiting boats when available there for loading?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I think there has been sufficient grain in position to fill all orders. The situation which developed out in Vancouver some time ago has been cleared up, and there is no trouble there now at all.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING UNEQUAL DELIVERY QUOTAS

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last, March 16, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) put to me the following question:
In a brief submitted to the Rand commission this morning, the Dominon Coal Company stated its intention to shut down three mines in Cape Breton, with the resulting lay-off of 2,557 miners. What action is the government planning in this regard?
In reply to this question, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that I have now inquired into the part of the brief submitted by the Dominion Coal Company to the royal commission on coal, with regard to the shutting down of certain coal mines in Cape Breton.
The brief does not specify when those three mines would shut down, but it does imply that they would not do so at the same time and that the closing would be spread over a certain period of time.
When the shut-down of a mine is being considered, formal notice must be given to the provincial government and an agreement must be reached with that government as to the date, safety measures and other factors.
I must add that neither the company nor the Nova Scotia provincial government has advised me of their intentions in this regard. In the circumstances, I think the hon. member for Villeneuve will agree that it is not part of my duties to anticipate future decisions of the provincial government or the findings of the royal commission on coal.
I can assure him, however, that all aspects of the coal mines problem in Nova Scotia are being carefully looked into. When the facts are clearly established, appropriate action will be considered and no doubt announced in due course.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must begin by expressing my regret at disappointing you.
On an occasion like this it is not always easy to decide what matters to bring to the attention of the house and the government. A very obvious question, of course, is defence policy. On that matter, Mr. Speaker, although the house has been in session now for more than two months, we have not yet had a word from the minister or the government in regard to defence policy.
We have now had nine departments put into supply, but the Department of National Defence is not included among those nine. We had a throne speech debate for some days during which there were several statements on defence matters from this side of the house, but no statement on defence policy was made by a representative of the government, either the Minister of National Defence or any other minister. We have had no white paper on defence, and I gathered from an interjection of the minister the other day, though it does not appear in Hansard, that we may not be getting a defence white paper this year.
It is true that we now have what by courtesy has been called a defence committee; but according to the Prime Minister it will not be permitted to discuss policy. The Prime Minister made that clear last January. However, the Minister of National Defence said last Thursday-and this introduces a note of ambiguity in an already ambiguous situation.-as reported on page 2182 of Hansard for March 17:
It is also my understanding that when my estimates are brought forward the leader of the house will move that they be referred to this committee. That would give this committee an opportunity to examine the estimates for the next year and to discuss therefore the policy that is being followed.
Yet on the very next day after that statement was made the minister had this to say, as reported on page 2221 of Hansard:
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made quite clear that those expenditures were to be considered in relation to the general policy, but that the general policy was not to be discussed.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the very essence of clarity in regard to the work of this so-called defence committee. When we on this side refuse to accept this kind of committee, with

the contradictory and confused statements made about it, the Minister of National Defence gets angry and accuses us of "whining and blubbering"-I think that was the expression used-when we object to a committee set up to discuss expenditures only for a particular period of time. The committee is not permitted to discuss defence policy. Therefore I hope that before long we will have a statement from the Minister of National Defence with regard to defence policy which might be the basis of a debate in this house. Certainly there can be no such discussion or debate in the so-called committee which has been set up.
There is another subject which indicates the fumbling and indecisive attitude of the government, and which is also a very good illustration of contradictory statements made by members of the government. I am referring to the subject of our international trade and balance of payments. This is a big subject, and although I may have to speak for some time I shall not of course be able to discuss all aspects of it. The government has left itself open to so much criticism that it would take many hours to deal with all its sins of omission and commission. What I omit will be dealt with by other hon. members on this side of the house.
With regard to this subject, unlike that of defence, we do have some information from government spokesmen. We heard an extraordinary speech by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on January 26 last. The minister will no doubt be replying to me in this debate. We also had a very important report by the governor of the Bank of Canada which deals with these matters, a report which in its terms challenges and contradicts the easy optimism of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as expressed in this house on January 26. If the Minister of Finance agrees with the views of the govern-nor of the Bank of Canada-and he has given some indication outside this house that he does-then surely the Minister of Finance will wish on an appropriate occasion to take advantage of the opportunity to deal in this house with the speech made by his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There are many precedents in this government for that sort of thing happening.
Let us look at the situation with regard to our international trade and balance of payments at the present time. In 1959, in our transactions in goods and services with other countries, Canada made several records; some very bad records indeed, which expose certain of the weaknesses in our economy at the present time to an extent which should provoke the concern of every member of this house. They have already provoked a great 79951-0-142

deal of concern outside of this house among businessmen, economists and others who are qualified to speak on these matters.
I shall mention some of these. First there is the question of our total liabilities, that is non-resident investments, either direct investments or investments in securities and bonds. We had a record here in 1959. The figure reads $24 billion, which represents a doubling of this total since 1952. Moreover-and this is the alarming feature-the rate of increase is rising. Second, there is the figure regarding net indebtedness, that is the difference between our liabilities and our assets. In this respect we established another record in Canada in 1959 of $15.4 billion, a figure which has more than tripled since 1952. Then there is the figure covering total deficit in current transactions in goods and services in 1959, another record; $1,460 million as against a surplus of $164 million in 1952.

speechtext:
It is slightly higher than the figure I have given. The deficit on current account transactions with the United States decreased slightly in the last year. But though this figure of our deficit with the United States was somewhat higher, in 1956 and 1957, it should not be forgotten that at that particular time we had a compensating surplus with regard to our overseas transactions. However, the figure was higher than in 1958, and it has now reached a point where it represents 85 per cent of our total deficit, that is our deficit with the United States. This shows or helps to show, because there are many other features which also show it, the measure of our dependence on the United States.
Even more disturbing than some of these figures, and certainly more significant, is the geographical distribution of our balances. The traditional surplus we have had in this country in our transactions with the United Kingdom and the sterling area has been reduced from $502 million in 1952 to $64 million in 1959, of which $52 million was a surplus with the United Kingdom and $12 million a surplus with the other countries of the commonwealth. Our balance with the
O.E.E.C. countries excluding, of course, the United Kingdom-and this is a very important area of our trade and one which is causing a good deal of trouble in the light of developments in Europe-has fallen from a surplus of $332 million in 1952 to a deficit of $149 million in 1959.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: But there is mutual aid in there, and things of that nature.

speechtext:
That is perfectly true, but the biggest figure for mutual aid was before 1952, with respect to the United Kingdom, when we made our $2 billion grant immediately after world war II. The figures for all the other countries except the United Kingdom, the O.E.E.C. countries and the commonwealth, have fallen from a surplus of $179 million in 1952 to a deficit of $139 million in 1959.
Summing up, then, our balances with countries other than the United States have changed from a surplus of $1,013 million in 1952 to a surplus of $49 million in 1958 and to a deficit of $224 million in 1959. Surely the minister will agree, as every hon. member in the house must agree, that this is a disturbing situation.
Equally disturbing is the present character of our net capital inflow. That has changed drastically in recent years. It is now directed more and more to the financing of our long

term debt. In 1957 only 15 per cent of our net capital inflow was directed to this purpose. In 1959 the figure was 30 per cent. On the other hand our net direct and portfolio investment-that is the direct portfolio investment of foreigners in Canadian concerns -which was 73 per cent of our net inflow in 1957 has fallen to only 41 per cent in 1959. This is the kind of investment which develops productive capacity in Canada and should add to our export capacity after the investment has taken place.

I am talking about direct portfolio investment and not necessarily equity ownership. I do not think my hon. friend's observation applies to this category at all.
In contrast, our short term capital imports are increasing. In 1957 they were only 12 per cent and in 1959 they were 29 per cent, a figure I mentioned only a few weeks ago in this house. Surely that is disturbing. That money comes into this country not to develop productive capacity in Canada and add to our export capacity, but comes in for speculative purposes and can be withdrawn as easily as it comes in.
In 1957 only 27 per cent of the capital inflow was designed to finance government and short term needs. In 1959, 59 per cent came in for these purposes and, as I have said, not to increase future production or export capacity. It is this inflow of capital, covering merchandise deficits which has kept the exchange value of our dollar up. The average value of the United States dollar in 1959 over the year was 95.90 per cent. In
1958	it was 97.06 per cent, and in 1957 it was about the same.
The result of that, of course, is obvious. It has encouraged imports into the country and has discouraged exports out of Canada. The reason for this is equally obvious. It has been due to the general monetary policy of the government, relatively higher interest rates, the tight money position here, and the scarcity of funds in Canada which forced the provinces and municipalities to have recourse to financing in the United States. I will have some figures on that subject a little later.
Let us look not at our general deficit position but at our merchandise deficit position. In
1959	it was $386 million, lower than 1956 and 1957.

speechtext: By quite a bit.

speechtext:
It is lower in those years,
but it is more than twice that of 1958. This arises from the fact that our exports in 1959 went up by about 5 per cent-I think just over or under that figure-and our imports went up by 9 per cent. It is quite true, as no doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce will point out when he speaks, that there has been an improvement in the last quarter of 1959, when there was actually a surplus. It is also true, as the dominion bureau of statistics in its "Quarterly Estimates of Canadian Balance of Interest Payments" points out on page 2, that there were very special and seasonal factors which accounted for this. Quoting from that report of the bureau, I find it warns that-
-export balance on commodity account in the quarter appears to have been affected by special factors-
-and one that comes immediately to mind is the steel strike and the effect it had on our exports and imports of that commodity. All these things should be viewed by every hon. member of the house as a disturbing situation, it is emphasized by the statistics I have mentioned, but it does not appear to be disturbing to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
All this merely reflects, he says, our rapid growth. He attempts to suggest that this has often been shown before, that it is just a natural and normal part of Canada's development. Let us look at our experience to see whether that kind of observation is founded on fact or on wishful thinking.
We had, of course, a series of almost uninterrupted trade deficits in the early years of this century, during which period we witnessed the opening up of the west, a terrific period of expansion during which our import needs were very great. Our deficit in those years was brought about primarily by the necessity for investment in this country to increase our export capacity especially from the west. But during the period 1915-52 we do not find that situation. The pattern changes during those years. We had trade surpluses in 32 of the 38 years in the period from 1915-52, and we had deficits in only 6 years in that period, namely 1920, 1929, 1930, 1931, 1950 and 1951.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the past experience of this country does not support the claim that we have not very much to worry about with respect to trade deficits because they are part of the normal pattern of the historical development of this country. In the period since 1952 imports have been more unstable than exports. The trend has been to increased merchandise trade deficits; there is no doubt about that. I am covering the 79951-0-142J
Trade Balance
period from 1959 to 1952, an interval during which both parties were in office. But what is more worrying than the actual figures is the thought that such deficits are ceasing to be directly related to industrial development in this country and to increasing its capacity to export.
I am sure the minister will respect the judgment of the former deputy minister of trade and commerce, Mr. M. W. Sharp, who in a speech delivered in Montreal on March 8, 1960 pointed out that-
-broadly speaking, the whole ot the increase in exports between 1952 and 1959, some $800 million, was offset by increased imports ol consumer goods alone.
He also pointed out that this increase in such imports had been distributed throughout all the categories of such goods. If that shows anything it shows that our increased exports have paid only for the imports designed to improve our consumer standard of living, and not to provide greater production and exports.

In this speech which Mr. Sharp made in Montreal he underlined another very disturbing feature about our exports, namely the narrow bases for the increase we have had in those years, an increase which I said was about $800 million, because $540 million of this $800 million increase is covered by three products which do not figure at all, or to any extent, in our export returns in 1952 or before. They are the three commodities which cover $540 million of the $800 million increase in our exports since 1952. Because so much of this increase

has been concentrated in these three categories it puts our export situation in a more vulnerable position that it otherwise would be.
We can all hope-and we hope our hopes will be realized-that gas and oil exports should continue to increase, but it will be very doubtful indeed whether they will increase enough to compensate for the decline in uranium exports. We also ask ourselves the question, what will be the effect of European developments in an area where our export figures are already disturbing? I am thinking now of the European free trade area, where tariffs are to be reduced by 20 per cent as of July. Within the area there is the European common market, where tariffs are to be reduced by 30 per cent, and a common tariff to be applied against all coutries outside the common market. Reference was made to that earlier this afternoon.
It is true that there are disturbing divisions of opinion in regard to this step which it is proposed to take, as between the United States on the one hand and the United Kingdom and other members of the free trade area on the other. If Canada does not share in the concessions which these groups are making among themselves, how can our exports expand in this market, especially if restrictions and obstructions on trade are placed on outsiders by those developing groups?
On the other hand, as Mr. Sharp said- and I quote again from his speech-
Our imports are going to be more resistant to downward adjustment than might have been expected.
Moreover, as we have seen, our nonmerchandise trade deficit has grown rapidly and regularly from $116 million in 1949 to $1,074 million in 1959, and unless pretty strong action is successfully taken it will continue to grow. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of immediate and deep concern. The longer we go on piling up deficits, huge deficits, the harder the ultimate problem of adjustment becomes and later moves, which will have to be made if this continues, will perhaps be more drastic. They may have the kind of undesirable economic, social and employment effects which we certainly want to avoid in any financial moves that we may have to make.
The Minister of Finance himself has warned us about this development; the governor of the Bank of Canada has certainly warned us in the annual report, in which he told us we are living beyond our means, and so have many others. It will be folly to ignore those warning signs. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the United States is not ignoring them, and the signs are not nearly so obvious in the United

States in respect of United States business as they are in Canada in respect of Canadian business. The over-all trade deficit in the United States in 1959 was $3.7 billion as against ours of $1.46 billion; and in terms of relative national income that is a much less serious situation than that which confronts us in Canada.
It is also different in the sense that the United States has, I believe, a commodity trade surplus, and that its deficit is due largely to its military and economic aid, in a way which is not the case in Canada. He did not seem particularly alarmed about the deficit. He said-I am paraphrasing, but I think this is reasonably accurate-that he would leave it to the economists to determine whether a deficit in a period of economic expansion is as serious as is sometimes made out. Perhaps he will also leave it to the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada, written by an economist who no doubt was assisted by economists. On March 10 in this house the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in answer to a question, I think, is reported on page 1920 of Hansard as having said:

I quote from pages 8 and 9 of the report, where it has this to say:
Three more years have gone by in which we have had very large balance of payments deficits, and we are now launched on another year with the prospective excess of total spending over production being greater than ever, presumably to be matched by an equivalent excess of imports which will have to be financed by foreign resources in one form or another.
The cumulative effect of all these developments must be to weaken the ability of the Canadian economy to meet the difficulties of the next recession to come upon us from abroad, and to make more likely the development of a domestic recession arising from excesses and structural strains

within our own economy, which may or may not coincide in timing with recession conditions abroad.
Then he went on to say:
Even if we were intent on trying to continue in that way, it must be recognized that in a capital-hungry world we cannot in fact count on having ready access to foreign capital year after year on a large scale. The longer the process of attempted overexpansion or over-rapid expansion goes on, the more maladjustments will be built into our economy, and the more difficult and painful will be the readjustments which will in time be forced upon us. We must in the end learn as a nation to live within our means, and exhibit the strength and will to do so. It would in my view be the path of realism to move firmly in that direction on a broad front without delay.
