That comment was made in 1956. He sounded that note of what the Leader of the Opposition calls gloom then. What action was taken by the government of that day?

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, instead of the minister asking me a question he has read another paragraph from the governor's report with which I also agree; but if the situation explained by the governor of the bank with respect to 1956 was dangerous then, it is far more dangerous now; and if the minister feels that something should have been done about it in 1956-we claim that something was done about it-the minister should be all the more worried and ready to do something about it now, when the governor says we are reaching a position of danger which was not the case to the same extent in those years. That is all the more reason why the minister should not be so complacent and optimistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: What was done in 1956?

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been pretty generous with my hon. friends in letting them interrupt. Perhaps they will let me go ahead with my statement, and the hon. gentleman can make his statement after the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes his.
I want to talk for some time about the objective of our trade policy, having given some statistics which should, I hope, convince the minister that all is not as rosy with that policy as he tries to indicate in his speeches. With the minister showing a kind

of blend of complacency and ignorance it is not surprising that there should be a good deal of confusion about the objectives and direction of our trade policy at this time. The traditional Tory protectionist approach has been shown in the woollen tariffs and so-called voluntary quota restrictions on Japanese goods. At a time when the ministers preach liberalism to foreign countries they have taken the arbitrary valuation powers under the 1958 revision of the Customs Act. They once even boasted about a 15 per cent diversion of trade as an objective of policy, as a direction of policy, but that proud policy is now reserved for Canadian speeches in Albert hall in London. It has declined from exaltation and exhortation to mere illusion. It is another disappearing vision.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Has there not been a diversion of about 12 per cent?

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
No, of course not. If the Prime Minister would really try to understand the trade statistics of his own officials he would surely not say that there has been a diversion of 12 per cent. A diversion of 12 per cent, within the meaning of the Prime Minister's original statement, would have meant that we would have transferred about $300 million of our imports from the United States to the United Kingdom. Have we done that? Let the Prime Minister look at the figures and find out for himself that we have not done that. On the contrary, we are more dependent on the United States than ever before.
Then, Mr. Speaker, if as the governor of the Bank of Canada says we must, as a nation, learn to live within our means, we must begin to balance our exports and imports and goods and services. How are we going to do that? We must do it by reducing our imbalance of current trade transactions, the imbalance about which I have been talking. There are two ways in which we can do that. The first is by reducing our non-merchandise deficit, and we know what that has reached this year. The second way is by changing our merchandise deficit into a surplus.
Let us take the first course first. This is not going to be easy to do, because the last year in which we had a non-merchandise surplus was 1948. I admit that fact. Let us take one item in our current non-merchandise deficit, the item of travel account with the United States. In 1948 we had a surplus in travel account of $148 million. In 1959 that has been changed to a deficit of $200 million, and it is growing. What are we going to do about that? Will we keep Canadians from going across the border or get more tourists
Trade Balance
from the United States to come into Canada? There is no choice, of course, between those two as objectives of trade policy.
Similarly, as another illustration of the difficulty, let us consider the current deficit on interest and dividends. In 1948 this amounted to $255 million, while in 1959 it is $486 million. It did go down in 1953 to $239 million, and in 1956 it was about $339 million. It has now gone up since 1952 by 26 per cent, until it has reached the present figure of $486 million. In 1959, the present year, sales abroad of new issues of Canadian securities reached the figure of $440 million, of which the provinces accounted for $279 million and the municipalities for $121 million. That also is a new record, and we know the effect that has had, I have already mentioned it, on the premium on our dollar. It is a very unhappy situation, surely when we are financing so much of our public services in this country by borrowing abroad and thereby increasing our over-all deficit through the payments of interest and principal which we have to make on those loans.
Has the government any ideas on how to reduce this non-merchandise deficit? I have mentioned travel expenses, and two ways of doing it; by encouraging those coming in and by control of those going out. The same thing applies, of course, to investments. No one in this country, I think, wants any control, certainly no unnecessary control except as a last resort, of foreign investment in this country. Nevertheless, when you quote this figure of $440 million in one year you realize that it is a pretty serious situation.
However, this would be a negative approach to this problem. A far more satisfactory approach, because it is a more positive approach, would be to transfer our current commodity deficit into a growing surplus to offset this non-merchandise deficit; that is what we have done in this country in the past. We have often had a surplus for that purpose. I have quoted the figures to show that.
How are we going to do that? A first possible way of doing it is by way of reducing our imports. The elimination of the premium on the dollar would help to do this as well as help to increase exports. The Minister of Finance has already indicated outside the house some of the obstacles in the way of doing that, the objections to it, and perhaps during the course of this debate some of those objections will be repeated in the house. It could be done, of course, by higher tariffs, quotas or other trade restrictions to reverse the trend of increased imports; and it has been a general trend. If that course of action were taken, not only

Trade Balance
would the restrictive action have to be drastic to be effective, but it would be undesirable and would be wrong. It would cause a further rise in the cost of living and especially a rise in the cost of production, thereby damaging our exports even if it did help our imports. It would prejudice, if not destroy, our position in GATT, and it would invite retaliation against us. This course, therefore, is not to be recommended.
The only desirable, logical, practical way is in the direction of increasing our exports. I am not going to stop there. I am going to try to indicate how, perhaps, that can be done. Faced with this situation, though in a much less serious way, this is exactly what the United States is doing at this time, as the minister must know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: And what we are doing, too.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: You are doing it in reverse.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Here is what the governor of the Bank of Canada says about it, and I quote from pages 12 and 13 of the governor's report:
United States policy has not sought to restrict the flow of imports for balance of payments reasons, nor to cut the total flow of foreign aid. Rather it has sought to increase exports-by improving competitiveness and strengthening sales efforts, and by pressing for the removal of foreign import restrictions-and to persuade other countries financially able to do so to look after a large share of the increased foreign aid requirements of underdeveloped countries.
This must be our policy too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: That is exactly what we have been doing.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Indeed, this is far more important for us than it is for the United States. We must realize that our export trade is more vulnerable, as well as being far more important to us, than the export trade of the United States. It is quite true that the index value of exports has gone up from its figure of 100 in 1948 to 163 in 1959. But the index of physical volume of export trade for the period 1948 to 1959 has gone up only to 134. Therefore, allowing for the rise in productivity in the export industries during those years, the employment content of our export trade has remained just about the same from 1948 to 1959. The lack of expansion in exports in these terms is a main cause of our chronic unemployment, as I have already said.
This might serve to modify some of the optimism which the Minister of Finance has been expressing in his muttered interventions in the last few minutes. Most of the increase, as 1 have pointed out, is due to three products, uranium, iron ore, and gas and oil,

and our traditional exports over the past years have not increased as they should have increased, especially since 1952.
Before the minister boasts about the recent increases he should recall, as I mentioned a few minutes ago, the dominion bureau of statistics explanation of this increase. He should take note of the warning in the Bank of Canada report, page 14, where Mr. Coyne says:
In a number of important respects, therefore, it seems likely that Canadian exports will be less assisted by specially favourable conditions than in the recent past and will have to depend more on ability to meet stiff competition in a world in which alternative sources of supply are now readily available. Even on the assumption of favourable developments in the trading policies of European and other countries, merely passive reliance on presumed natural advantages cannot be expected to improve or indeed even to maintain our position in world trade.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it all adds up to the fact that we may be approaching nothing less than a crisis in our international trade and balance of payments position. The government has to face up to this problem and do something about it. Basically it is a problem of finding increasing markets for the products of our present excess capacity. Having excess capacity-and we are very fortunate in having it if we can use it-means that exports could be increased without additional investments or additional foreign capital, and that itself would greatly improve our balance of payments position. More than ever in this country an expanding volume of exports, must be the main objective of Canadian trade policy.
What is the government going to do to bring that about? I know that they will say, "Well, what would you do?" That is the reply of the government to every question of this kind which we ask. I will mention certain things which in my view should be done.
First and foremost we must adopt a sensible tariff policy. We must realize that if we are going to sell, because we are an exporting country, we have to buy, and we must be particularly careful in our trade and tariff relations with a country like Japan which represents an important developing and, we hope, permanent market in the future for our primary products. But it is a market which we can easily lose because we are selling products in this market which the Japanese can get from other parts of the world unless, we are careful in our diplomatic negotiations with them with regard to Japanese exports to this country. It is quite true, as someone said the other day, that while we must buy Canadian, other things being equal, even more we must sell Canadian.

Second, we must adopt a more aggressive export trade promotion policy. The government foreign trade services should be enlarged and improved and we should start sending selling missions to the world instead of the type of buying mission which we sent in 1957. We must be more effective and agres-sive in our trade negotiations.
Let me mention one commodity, uranium, which represented $320 million of export trade last year. When that trade hung in the balance, as it did during 1959 because of the attitude of the United States, what happened? We had a return the other day and that return showed that in this particular situation when representations should have been made to the United States on the highest level to maintain that trade there was one dispatch from the government of Canada through the embassy in Washington signed by charge d'affaires ad interim to the secretary of state. That is the only document in two years which represented formal official representations to the government of the United States in respect of a commodity which last year represented in our export table $320 million.
This is also an obvious thing to say, but it is important. We must improve our competitiveness by keeping our costs of production down. That does not mean only that there should be no wage increases which are not justified by increased productivity. That is an important matter, but it is only one element; it is not the only element. It is not even the only important element in costs of production, though it certainly is one. Keeping our costs of production down means also avoiding excessive profits both in the operation and in the formation and financing of companies. It means avoiding excessive taxation and preventing, so far as government can help prevent, administrative pricing arrangements by big corporations which prevent the play of economic and competitive forces on prices; arrangements which prefer high prices even if less volume, to lower prices and greater volume.
Then we have to improve our competitive position by expanding our export credit facilities. I know the government took steps last year to this end, but I would like to hear from the minister how those steps are working out and what has been the result of these increased export credit facilities. Very often, as I am sure the minister knows, sales are lost and permanent trade relationships are not established, not because of price or quality of Canadian goods but because our competitors are able to give better credit terms. This is all the more serious a problem at the present time because 79951-0-143
Trade Balance
of the steps which the United States government is now taking to improve its credit facilities, and we will have to consider meeting those steps.
May I mention one other way in which we can push exports; that is by pushing the exports of natural gas to the United States. There have been long delays in this matter due to legal and administrative difficulties created, in part at least, by the Canadian government itself. In June, 1959 when the energy bill was introduced the Prime Minister promised at that time early action in respect of this matter. It is now nearing the end of March 1960 and no action has yet been taken.
Another thing which has to be done is to continue the assault on non-tariff obstacles to exports. Customs procedures, administrative regulations, arbitrary valuations, health and quarantine regulations; all these things create uncertainty, delay and expense. We came up against that when we were in office and I know that the government has come up against it since it has been in office. I know that the government has taken steps to correct this situation, but surely more can be done now than was possible in the past. In dealing with these matters, which can at times be worse than tariffs themselves as obstacles to our exports, this kind of change can be made without there being any danger of infringing any of the rules of GATT.
It is time to push these changes with the United States more vigorously perhaps than we have in the past, because the United States, now warned by their own trade balances, are beginning to push this complaint of administrative protection in other countries. Therefore they may be a little more receptive to vigorous representations from Canada now than they have been over the years. Perhaps now is a good time to impress upon them that postprandial expressions of sympathy and understanding of Canada's problems are not enough, and try to convince them that if they cannot help us in these matters, our increasing difficulties will hurt them more than ever before; because we are now by far their best customer, both for goods and for investments, I think it is fair to say that our negotiating position with the United States today, certainly in this field, is stronger than it has ever been.
These are some things which I suggest could and should be done. But they themselves will not be enough to meet the long range dangers ahead which require long range solution. This long range danger, which has perhaps at times been overshadowed in our minds by our short range difficulties, is due to the development in the world of

Trade Balance
economic regionalism, the emergence of these great new trading blocs. We have two now in western Europe; we have the common market with its overseas affiliates in Africa, and we have the free trade area of seven European countries. This move is extending to Latin America where they are discussing a Latin American free trade area. In fact they are more than discussing it; I may be wrong in this, but I believe they are on the verge of drawing up a treaty to that effect. They are discussing a Central American free trade area. I read not long ago that negotiations have begun for a preferential system of trade between all Arab countries. A southeast Asia economic association is being talked about; and we all know about the communist bloc and its concentrated regional effort to interfere with our trade and our exports.
All this means that perhaps instead of the multilateral world to which we have been accustomed since world war II we are approaching and moving into the world of giant regional economic blocs competing with those outside those blocs not only in the sale of manufactured goods but in the purchase of raw materials. I wonder how long the most favoured nation principle and the principle of non-discrimination can persist in the face of a developing situation of this kind. Our own position is as vulnerable as that of any other country in the world if such a development takes place. It is perhaps more exposed than any other country in the world. While the United States can be hurt by this kind of thing, it cannot be hurt nearly as much as we can.
We are just beginning to realize how much one of the blocs could hurt not only Canada but all the countries of the free world. I am speaking now about the communist bloc. We have learned in the last year or two that the U.S.S.R. and its trade satellites, with trade controlled from one central office, are in a good position to compete successfully with our traditional exports. Even though they might lose financially in the competition, they are willing to accept that loss for reasons which have nothing to do with trade. They can do that and disrupt normal trade channels to our disadvantage. We are just beginning to see the effect of this. Although there has been relatively little damage as yet, we have learned from what has been done what might happen if more were attempted. And Canada, as I have said, is very vulnerable.
Mr. Khrushchev no doubt had this idea in mind when he said: "We will bury you." He meant that the Soviet union would bury the free nations in the peaceful field of trade conducted under the rules of the Soviet union,

and these are not likely to be Marquis of Queensberry rules. I doubt whether we shall be able to compete very successfully with this kind of aggressive trading, if and when it takes place, through national competitive trading policies organized on the basis of exclusive competing nation states.
It seems to me that the United States, again, has seen the dangers of this situation more clearly than we have in this country, although I know that the Prime Minister has made some strong statements with regard to it. It was the under secretary in the United States, not the Secretary of State for External Affairs in Canada (Mr. Green) nor the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) who initiated the talks with the O.E.E.C. countries in December to lay the groundwork for Atlantic economic co-operation. This, as has been pointed out by the government, is a very important development, and this next meeting in Paris on April 19 may prove a very significant one for the future or our country and for our whole system of trading.
It is not easy to be optimistic about early tangible results. If the United States and Canada remain outside the common market *-and I do not see how any other result could happen immediately-it will be impossible under GATT for the six nations of the common market or the outer seven to grant us any special concessions, especially as their area will take in some of the colonial and trust territories of Africa. Perhaps the only good result we have any right to expect from this development at the present time is a general reduction of tariffs inside these two groups which would be applicable to all the countries of GATT, and it is not likely that this can be done now on any material scale.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Can that be done within GATT?

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: Yes, it would be quite possible. I understand that the common market is giving consideration at the present time to that aspect, but it will have to be applicable to all members of GATT or they will be breaking the GATT regulations.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: So it really cannot be done within GATT.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
It could be done, but perhaps we would be unrealistic if we expected too much from that kind of development at the present time. But we have every reason to expect that the common market is likely to become much more self-sufficient. Unless something more far-reaching happens than has now occurred we may well find that not

only manufactured goods but raw material from overseas areas will be competing with our own.
That need not happen. If the common market countries so desired, they could remove obstructions against trade between themselves and the outside world rather than increase them, and I hope that will be done, but it would be unrealistic to think that is bound to occur, and it would be very unrealistic to evade the possibility of dangerous consequences.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking on this subject earlier this session, said:
The future of Canada's external trade appears bright. The prospects are for substantial increases in Canada's exports and for further diversification of our foreign trade.. . our exports are expected to grow at a more rapid pace.
I do not believe this optimistic assessment of the present position is likely to be borne out by the facts. I hope I will be wrong in this, and I hope I will not be accused of being a prophet of doom and gloom because I bring these dangers forward. I am basing my views in part on those of people outside politics who have studied this question and who have made a sober assessment of the prospects before us. I refer particularly to the governor of the Bank of Canada.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), in a speech in Saskatoon on February 20, had this to say:
We must also keep in mind .. . the importance of preserving the world-wide multilateral trading system which has been so patiently and successfully constructed over the past 12 years.
That in itself is a compliment to the trade policy of the preceding government; to say that over the years we have patiently and successfully built up a multilateral trading system. I think that statement is true, but I suggest that the situation is changing, and I am not so sure that it is going to be possible to maintain this system for the next 12 years based, as it is, on the foundation of GATT. Of course, we must try to retain this foundation of the multilateral system, but if that system declines through no fault of ours, what are we going to do? These questions have been raised by another authority on the subject outside this house, and I should like to quote the words of Professor Deutsch spoken in Montreal on March 8:
One of the more disturbing problems which arise from recent developments is the difficult choice which they pose for countries such as Canada, Japan and for many small nations around the world. Canada has built her post-war policy on the multilateral and most favoured nation principle. Should Canada now seek to align herself more closely with some regional group, none of which could provide a satisfactory arrangement? Should it be toward Europe or toward the United States? Is it
79951-0-1431
Trade Balance
possible to build a wider Atlantic association into which Canada could fit? Or, failing this should Canada seek to go it alone in the hope that reasonably liberal international policies can be made to prevail?
These are some of the questions which the changing objectives and changing trends in world trade pose for us today, and in the years to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: You did not answer any of the questions.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
The government is in a
better position than anybody to try to answer these questions because the government has the responsibility of dealing with them. We are bringing these questions and problems to the attention of the government in the hope that we may get a statement of government policy with regard to the search for a solution of them.
These are the problems. What is the approach of the government toward their solution, aside from cheerful and optimistic surveys?
The ultimate objective, we agree, is the freest possible trade on a universal basis. For Canada it is more imperative than ever to have an expanding and diversified trade, for the reasons I have indicated earlier. Otherwise we will continue to live beyond our means while an increasing part of our resources will be unemployed. That really spells disaster. The immediate problem is how to reconcile this reliance on the multilateral approach through GATT with a world which, whether we like it or not, is moving toward regionalism.
Can we avoid this trouble? Can this problem be solved by continuing to rely on the principles and practices of the multilateral approach of the past? In such a situation how do we increase our exports and maintain our domestic industries against new and aggressive regional competition and communist trade movements? Can we possibly go it alone? Can we isolate ourselves in a world divided into giant economic blocs or will we be inevitably forced into our own special kind of bloc, complete economic integration with the United States? I do not think anyone in this house wants that to happen, but even if it did how would that guarantee the essential expansion of our exports?
Recent trade developments show that we are rapidly being faced with some categorical imperatives. Isolation is impossible. Increasing dependence on the United States is not a tolerable solution. We cannot improve the situation by joining the Six or Seven as presently organized. What, then, is the long range solution? As I see it the only one that appears to fit the developing situation

Trade Balance
is an Atlantic free trade area including the common market countries, the European free trade area and the United States.

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext: What about Japan?

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
The formation of an association such as an Atlantic free trade area would leave us free to determine our relations with other countries as we wished just as the members of the European free trade area are now in a better position to determine their relationships with other countries outside of that area including Japan. I know the difficulties and complexities of this. I am not putting it forward as some pat solution that can be found in the next 12 months. I know there would have to be a gradual adjustment over a period of years as is the case in Europe now and it would have to be done by stages; but I also know that a few years ago when we talked in this house about the development of the European common market and the European free trade area-and my friend the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will remember this-there was a general feeling that it would take years before it could be brought about, that political and economic reasons would make it almost impossible to accomplish inside a generation. But look at what has happened in the last two years.
We have reached the point now that on July 1 of this year the common market countries will take steps that in their earlier draft arrangements were not expected to take place until 18 months after July. Things are moving and while it will take a long time to accomplish these larger measures, if they can ever be accomplished, surely it would be a good thing to start the process now.
I am not, of course, asking the government for a commitment in favour of an Atlantic free trade area at this time. That would be quite unrealistic. I am asking the government, however, to give immediate, careful and complete consideration to this possibility, to get the best men in the country studying the possibility of an Atlantic free trade area on instructions from the government. If the results of these studies show that it can be done and that it is desirable that it be done, I urge the government to take the initiative in pressing this matter before the European countries. That is what is being done now by the United States. That is why Mr. Dillon went to Europe last December and was instrumental in calling this meeting.
There is no reason on earth why Canada should not at least associate itself in this initiative in an aggressive and formal way. It seems to me there is a real urgency in this matter. This is the time to do it if it is
going to be done at all. The European countries are finalizing their respective trade arrangements and next year it might be too late for any alternative proposal to be made to them.
There are new problems, new challenges and new opportunities, and so I ask the government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce in particular: What are you going to do? If you cannot give immediate and sympathetic consideration to the gradual establishment of an Atlantic free trade area, will you please tell the house why and give us an alternative which will meet the situation we are facing today, one that will prevent that situation developing into a danger and perhaps even into a crisis that will further weaken our balance of payments position and reduce our prosperity and check our growth as a nation. Of one thing I am certain, and it may be paradoxical. If we want to become less dependent we have to become more interdependent.
May I sum up, Mr. Speaker, by saying that our grave concern as to the deterioration in Canada's trading position arises from:
1.	A record deficit of nearly $1.5 billion in total trade.
2.	A record deficit of nearly $1.1 billion in non-merchandise trade.
3.	A $1.2 billion dollar deficit in our trade with the United States.
4.	A rapidly declining favourable balance with the United Kingdom and other sterling area countries-$64 million in 1959 as compared with $502 million in 1952-and growing deficits with all other trading areas.
5.	A record $15 billion net debt abroad.
6.	Stagnation in the volume of our traditional exports.
7.	The financing of a growing proportion of Canada's unfavourable balance by imports of capital which do not increase Canada's capacity to export.
8.	The emergence of trading blocs throughout the world threatening to isolate Canada from important markets.
Therefore, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house expresses its grave concern at the deterioration in Canada's trading position as emphasized by an unfavourable balance of nearly $1.5 billion in Canada's total trade in 1959, and urges the government to deal with this serious problem by taking effective action, including the working out of proposals for the establishment on a gradual and progressive basis of an Atlantic free trade area."

maintopic: TRADE-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO REMEDY UNFAVOURABLE BALANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to repeat many of the worth-while arguments and interesting statistics that have just been given the house
[Mr. Pearson.)

by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) on this important subject of trade and Canada's position both as an exporting and importing nation. I thing we all agree that Canada is facing a great challenge. I feel certain from reading editorials in recent newspapers that the press and through them the people are very much concerned as to what is taking place and are expecting that the government benches here in Ottawa will meet this challenge and let them know how serious the situation actually is and what the government has in mind to deal with problems of the future as far as Canada is concerned.
I was interested in a recent editorial carried in the Timmins Press which concluded with these words:
The time has come for Prime Minister Diefen-baker and Finance Minister Fleming to tell us where we are heading and what is being done about it.
You can go not only to Timmins but to every leading newspaper in Canada and you will find the worries that are in their minds and the demands for government explanation and government action.
There can be no question that the government, through its highly placed civil servants and the analyses they must be making of the reports of industrialists, financiers and economists, has had some warning as to the development of the present situation, some warning as to the grave development that might face us in the future. I just wish to make a brief mention of two that I noted in a speech made to the economic forecast panel of the Vancouver board of trade on November 23 last by Mr. O. J. Firestone, economic adviser to the Department of Trade and Commerce, who had some very pertinent comments to make. In view of the most influential position he holds, surely what he had to say there has been studied by the minister and by the government and that therefore we are entitled to know what they are doing about the analyses which have been presented to them.
I am not going to take the time of hon. members to read it, although I think it might be worth while if all could read the statement made by Mr. Firestone in November of last year in my home city of Vancouver, but I would just point out that he did say there were very serious problems ahead. He outlined some of those problems as being export problems. It is noticeable that what Mr. Firestone put at top priority in discussing export problems was to a great extent the same matter which the Leader of the Opposition has just been drawing to the attention of the government and of the house.
Trade Balance
Mr. Firestone very definitely pointed out that the creation of trading blocs, such as the common market, the outer seven, the Central American common market and increasing reliance on bilaterial trade agreements would tend to limit the opportunities of Canadian businessmen to sell increasing quantities of our products abroad. He also pointed out- it was touched upon very briefly by the Leader of the Opposition-the problem of the premium on the Canadian dollar. He emphasized at that time that the high premium on the Canadian dollar has been creating problems for our industries, both those catering to the export market and those catering to the home market. I feel that we need a real explanation from the Minister of Finance, and perhaps from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), as to the ultimate effect of our high premium dollar and as to whether it would be advisable for Canada to consider its relation to our financial situation.
There can be no question at all that if we are to maintain and to increase our exports we have to deal with the cost of production and productivity. Of course, related to that are all those things that make up the total cost of produce in Canada which will of necessity include profits and wages. All of these things have an impact and we are hoping that as a result of their studies the government will be in a position in this two-day debate to give an honest and factual picture of Canada's trade situation today, how they think it will be tomorrow and the year after, without doing any wishful thinking, and how they are planning to meet the problem.
We all know, and it should be accepted as axiomatic that Canada is an exporting nation. We are a very large country with a relatively small population. Therefore, we cannot maintain an economic self-sufficiency because we have not the consumer market that can cope with our productivity. Neither can we produce on an efficiency level with countries like the United States because that country does have a consumer market consisting of 180 million people. Therefore, we have to rely, or place a greater emphasis in our thinking, on exports. In my estimation at least we are now in, or facing, a most difficult situation and so far we have not heard of any government planning to take care of the problem which is now arising.
If we are honest we recognize the absolute necessity that compelled the inner six to form that group. Their economy, their desire for higher standards for their people necessarily drove them into that organization; but it is going to have a deep impact

Trade Balance
on Canada because not only are they working out free trade among themselves but they are doing something which a combination of capitalist countries have never done before. They are planning their economy; they are planning their productivity; they are planning their manufacturing according to the location and the country that can produce the highest quality and the greatest quantity with the greatest efficiency at the lowest price. That kind of planning is bound to have a great effect on their cost of production, on their rate of quality and quantitative productivity, and place them in a position of competition far greater than it has been in the past.
Because of that recognition, I feel sure that many companies in the United States and in the United Kingdom are no longer relying on being able to export from their own factories in their own countries. They are establishing factories in the countries of the inner six in order to be sure that if they cannot make profits on producing in their own countries and exporting, they can make profits by producing and selling in the countries of the inner six. This is just a simple fact. These are the facets of the case, and this is bound to have an effect on Canada.
I think we should hear from the great planners across the way as to how in an unplanned economic system in Canada they are going to meet a planned system of private enterprise in the inner six, because this is the situation. We are not going to feel the impact at the moment but I would say that inside of a few months, or a year, we certainly will feel it.
To a considerable extent we rely on our exports overseas. There is also the fact that we have not been facing up to the problem. This is because there has not been planning in Canada, planning of production, planning of exports and planning of imports. Already the situation is getting serious. I come from the province of British Columbia where we are so dependent on our lumber exports. May I emphasize again, as I have pointed out before, that seven years ago we shipped 200 per cent more lumber to the United Kingdom than did the U.S.S.R. while in 1959 the U.S.S.R. shipped 250 per cent more lumber to the United Kingdom than was shipped from the province of British Columbia. There has been a complete reversal of the trade picture. That is only the start of the economic cold war on the part of the U.S.S.R. From all I have been able to read it appears that within the next five years at the latest the U.S.S.R., if it so desires, will be able to go almost anywhere in the world and meet any price not only for lumber but also for metals and agricultural products.

It is no good waiting until that day arrives before we in Canada decide what we are going to do about the situation. I think a great service has been done our country by the forthright manner in which Mr. Coyne has outlined the problems as he sees them. I am not going to refer to the report itself because hon. members all have a copy of it. The Leader of the Opposition also made some excellent comments on it a few moments ago. But I should like to give the house the editorial comment of the Victoria Times on Thursday, March 17. This is what the Times had to say in an editorial headed "The Rake's Progress":
In plain terms Mr. Coyne tells the Canadian people they have been sowing the wind and, in due season, will reap the whirlwind. This warning does not come from a politician who must comfort or alarm the public to secure its votes. It comes from the non-partisan governor of the Bank of Canada, a great public servant with no axe to grind. If we continue our present course, Mr. Coyne believes, we shall not only be in a weak state to meet any business recession imported from the world but may well produce a domestic recession of our own.
Without referring to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Coyne flatly rejects Mr. Churchill's cheerful assurance that our gigantic and growing foreign debt is nothing to worry about. Also, Mr. Coyne's courageous report may help the Canadian people to see that their "easy-going illusions'' are leading them toward the gravest kind of trouble, may persuade us all, in Mr. Coyne's final words, to "stand on our own feet". Standing on foreign loans which may dry up at any time, we are due for a painful fall.
I cannot find any words of my own to highlight the situation better than the editorial comment of the Victoria Times on Mr. Coyne's report. We have got to face up to the world situation. We have got to face up to the new developments that are taking place around the world. We have got to face up to the fact that we in Canada must face reality. We would like to hear from the government whether they are going to face up to realities, whether they are going to face up to the hard facts even though they may be cruel and do some definite planning. As long as we continue to live under our present unplanned system we will continue to run into trouble and difficulties such as are now being experienced in our country.
I know that the government, the official opposition and the majority of people generally do not like controls but when controls are needed for the social good then controls should be brought into effect. We are not going to face up to the realities of the import and export situation by relying completely on a laissez-faire policy. I think the time has come when we have to consider import and export controls in an endeavour to balance that phase of our economy. If we are going to maintain the living standards of our people,

if we are going to increase those standards, which everybody desires, then it can only be done by not letting increased costs, increased wages and all other costs outstrip the productivity of the Canadian people. Productivity has to be ahead of increasing costs and that cannot be done if the matter is left to individual, regional or provincial action.
There has to be greater assistance from government sources in research and planning so as to bring the productivity of Canadian industry to the highest possible level. I say that if we do not do these things we will continue to be in the same position in which we are today and have been for some time. We are losing some of our markets already; for example, our market for lumber in the United Kingdom. In January of this year 2,300 men were left without work because there was no way we could dispose of herring caught off the British Columbia coast. This year the whaling fleet is not going out at all. We are familiar with the difficulties at Elliot Lake. Ten days from now the last coal mine on Vancouver island is shutting down. We are letting these things develop and continue because of the unplanned situation-I cannot say "policy" because I do not know how you can have an unplanned policy-in Canada.
I know I have the bad habit of reiteration but I do reiterate that the government is not, cannot and will not face up to our present deficit and the export-import situation unless it will come forward with a policy of planning for agriculture, finance, exports and imports. We find people in Canada having to go out of business or being bought out by outsiders and at the same time we are importing the very things that we are denying our own people the right to be able to produce. They are unplanned imports, if you want to put it that way.
I was invited out to dinner last week and I was most interested in looking over the shelves in the pantry. I was so interested that I picked up a couple of the items. They show what I mean by not planning. We felt like having some frozen strawberries. No finer strawberries are produced anywhere in the world than in Canada and particularly in the Fraser valley, but look at what has happened to the strawberry industry in British Columbia. In a supermarket in Ottawa we got some fresh frozen strawberries and I immediately assumed that they were Canadian strawberries because they were the famous York brand. It is a Canadian company well known across Canada. But these were whole strawberries, fresh frozen, fancy brand, product of Holland. Since when did we import strawberries from Holland? Right on the next shelf there was another famous Canadian brand,
Trade Balance
Aylmer. These strawberries were packed in the United States for Canadian Canners Limited. However, that company was bought out by United States interests and plants were closed down. Now produce is brought into our country and the Canadian brand name is used.
Why is it that we have an unplanned state where our own people go out of business because they cannot sell and at the same time we have a big deficit between exports and imports because we are importing products like these? I can go on with others.
I like cream in my coffee, and a lot of other people do, too. We have had a lot of trouble getting rid of powdered milk, have we not? We have given it away. Then why in the name of heaven do we adopt the policy under which we import powdered cream? You will find it is on the shelves of the stores in Ottawa. I am just bringing these things up as examples of not planning, not thinking, to keep our own people at work. In order to do this we should have some control of imports and we should recognize the absolute essentiality of importing things a little different from these.
Then there is the declared policy of the government to develop trade within the commonwealth. We have another company which is well known in the country, Honey Dew. It is very well known, and you will find it in Ottawa. This is Honey Dew orange juice. Why buy this when we have commonwealth countries that are crying for assistance which grow the finest oranges in the world? These are things we can think about, changes we can make to assist the commonwealth, to assist our own people and to bring our import position to a more realistic point. These are some of the things we ask the government to think about. These are some of the things upon which we are asking the government if they will kindly explain their policy. Will they tell us how they are facing up to the grave danger which now confronts our country from abroad?
Canada is facing a terrific challenge, a challenge that has to be met. The only ones who have the ultimate power of formulating policies to meet the challenge are the government, through their thinking and planning, and then tying that thinking and planning into a selling job to the Canadian people to aid Canadian labour, Canadian industry and Canadian agriculture. We are asking the government if they will make an announcement of their thinking and their policies.
I am not going to continue in this vein, but we do feel that the amendment introduced by the official opposition is not

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the statements that have beeen made today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the last speaker. I should like to refer to the last speaker's remarks concerning planning. He went into a great amount of detail about the fact that this government should plan for these economic things. I thought that probably after his trip to Asia this year, and the observations he made concerning foreign trade, he had probably changed a little bit. I think his observations which were made upon his return from Asia were the truest words I have ever heard him speak. He said that labour had to take its share of responsibility for our foreign trade. I think this is most important, and is one of the reasons for Canada losing a great deal of her foreign markets.
The last speaker also made reference to planning by governments. I should like to

point out to him that planning by governments, the former government and the other governments in the world, is greatly responsible for the trouble we are in, if we are in trouble. I do not believe we are in nearly as bad shape as the Leader of the Opposition portrayed today. During the war this country developed its industrial capacity to a great extent. After the war there was a great shortage of manufactured commodities in the world, so we were able to retain some markets and get into other markets.
However, the former minister of agriculture led us down the garden path during the last war, and this can be confirmed by asking any of the western members. He said, we will ship our wheat to England, and I agree that we should ship our wheat to England. However, the farmer alone was asked to accept a price which was about half the price of wheat on the world markets. The farmers were given assurance that after the war was over we would be able to retain these markets.
We know what nonsense that was because no one can afford to pay more than the price of the world market which existed at that time. I think that was one of the greatest injustices ever done to the farmers of Canada. They bore the brunt at $1.55 a bushel when industry and labour were getting their large cut of the profits. I wonder what would have happened if the labourer had been told; "We are going to send these armaments to help England; will you take instead of $2 an hour, $1 an hour for your labour?" That is exactly what the former administration did to the farmers. Through that we lost the rest of our markets. Consequently it has been a big effort to get them back.
I remember being in England in 1949 and asking for some cheese to go with a piece of apple pie. I asked for old Canadian cheese, and they brought me a piece of cheese that looked like a cross between margarine and butter. It had no flavour and I complained. I said, "Where is that good Canadian cheese for which we built up a market and a high reputation?", and they said, "Well, the government is doing the dealing now. It comes in and is sent out; there is no classification, grading, or anything else." Now, that is not the fault of the former administration, but what I am trying to point out is interference by another government in ordinary business channels.
I would like to give another instance. The other day when the Leader of the Opposition was talking about the uranium industry in Canada and our dealings with the United States with regard to that very important product he stated that this government could

have put pressure on them because the United States had a moral obligation to buy our uranium for a further period beyond the terms of the contract. I ask him as a business man, would he expect the United States to be buying it from the mines of Canada when the mines of the United States would probably be closed? We have to be realistic, and I was surprised when he referred to it again today.
Frankly, I lay a lot of the blame for our uranium industry and the export business it involves on the former administration, because they went out and took over these mines-I am referring to Eldorado, a crown corporation-and went along making contracts and interfering with the ordinary business channels. I do not think the former administration had any business to get into Eldorado and making it a crown corporation.
The former speaker talked about planning. I do not adhere at all to his views, and I had hoped that he and his group were being a little more tolerant toward this planning business. Frankly, I do not believe that governments can plan economic matters the way he thinks they can, unless we all want to go back and exist on the same basis as the people in Russia are existing.
East fall I went from Germany into Czechoslovakia. I went from a free enterprise country into one which is 97 per cent state operated, and frankly I wish that the former speaker could have seen the difference in those two countries, where you have planning on one hand and the free enterprise system on the other. In the eastern part of Germany you saw farms the like of which I defy anyone to see any place I have been, Canada included. I have never seen such good production and orderly, clean farms. Then you go into the other country where they are on a larger scale, and it was obvious, because it was harvest time, that there was a great difference between the two.
Before the last war Czechoslovakia was one of the greatest industrial countries and exported a great deal to this country. I wish you could see it today. I asked questions of different people who knew I was from Canada, and where there was no chance of any leak they told me that the people in Czechoslovakia are very unhappy today. I would like to say to the former speaker that I do not want to see any part of such plan in Canada.
I also believe that the businessmen can handle our exports more efficiently than any government branch or service. It is true the government is doing more business at the
Trade Balance
top level than businessmen are. For example, before 1940 there was a very healthy export business in wheat, flour and feed grains which was conducted by the grain brokers. Although I have not seen the figures, I believe we were getting a better share in world trade under that system than we are today under this crown corporation method. Mind you, I do not know a great deal about what happened before but I was in Europe last year and met one member from the wheat board and its European representative in two or three different countries, and I think those men are doing an exceptionally good job. I met them in the Near East at Istanbul, I met them in Greece and also in Austria. I was in 22 countries last fall and I met most of the trade representatives, and I would like to pay a compliment to that part of our government service. I think they are men who are dedicated to the job and are doing everything in their power; but frankly, with our cost of living and standard of living today in Canada, we are trying to keep up with our good neighbour to the south and I think it is leading us into a great deal of trouble.	1
Take our extravagance in the credit field. We have heard it said last week, why are we so short of credit? All you have to do is to look at the consumers' credit, the amount of money going into things people are buying on a credit basis. I think we have to get back to the spirit of some of our good Scottish ancestors and operate within our means.
I think there is a good deal too much dependence today on the government, a tendency which I abhor. We see it every day in this house. People come in to me in my riding and say, with regard to some local problem: what is the government going to do about this? It is the same with our businessmen. Our industries have built up a gigantic production of goods which they were able to sell in Canada, and they have not gone out on their own to seek markets abroad to the extent they should. I have talked to trade commissioners in South America, particularly, and they tell me that they have sent requests to certain industries asking whether they would be interested in exporting a particular product. In a number of cases the Canadian industry approached did not even answer the letter. Why? It was because after the war business was good and manufacturers could sell all their production in Canada. Consequently, they did not go to seek other markets.
The most important factor in our loss of markets is the cost of labour. I was in the exporting business after the war, and I was

Trade Balance
one of those who could find business easily in practically every place in the world because there was a great shortage of production. But when Germany and Japan got into the market-and what a recovery those countries made-we soon saw the realities of the situation. I was interested in a quotation on a ship in Venezuela in 1952. It was a comparatively small ship for one of the Canadian yards. We were beaten by the Germans on that quotation by nearly one third. Why? Because of their lower labour rate. In 1952 I was in a plant in Germany with as high a standard of labour as anywhere in the world. The top rate for machinists and other skilled employees was 55 cents an hour, whereas we in our yard in Canada were paying $1.85 an hour. When labour costs constitute such a large part of the cost of the manufactured article, how can we compete in these circumstances? I think organized labour has some very smart men and I frankly do not know why they cannot see that they are pushing us right out of the foreign market by these demands for higher and higher wages.
There is one other reason why, in my opinion, we have priced ourselves out of the foreign market, and that is our cost of government. If hon. members figure that out of every dollar of profit the federal government takes approximately 50 cents, the provincial government takes another piece and then the municipal government takes a further share, they will realize that if this burden were reduced, say by half, we could reduce the price of the individual article that we are trying to sell on the foreign market by a substantial amount. I agree with the fiscal policy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) 100 per cent. I think he has done everything he can possibly do, but I believe-and I admit that this expression has become a little hackneyed-we have inherited a lot of these troubles, and I am not very sure that the trend can be changed, because it is very difficult to back up, to turn the wheels of expenditure backward. The big question today is certainly whether we are living too extravagantly.
There is one field in which I do believe a certain amount of blame lies with the former administration, and that is in relation to our dealings with the United States, though, as I say, I often wonder how much any government really influences the trend of economic forces. Nevertheless, I see things in our tariffs which disturb me; cases where an article can enter Canada at a much lower rate of duty than it can enter the United States. One example which occurs to me, is that of chickens. A pound of chicken or
[Mr. Cathers.l
broiler, for example, can come into Canada from the United States and pays only three cents duty. If we ship a pound of chicken into the United States a duty of five cents a pound has to be paid. Soybeans and onions are other examples, and I could probably name dozens of commodities with regard to which there is a disparity between the rates. I should like to ask the Leader of the Opposition what his government did to correct these differences when it was in office. I know that our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and our Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) have made some corrections in this field, and I am pressing them to continue their efforts.
I think we are going through a period of transition. This is the natural effect of the war. We built up our production; we lost our markets during the war, and now we have got to get down to hard work and restore those markets. I am one of those who are realistic about this question, and I say it is not going to be easy because we are in competition with Russia, for example, which does not need to maintain anywhere near the standard of living or the freedom that we have. Russia can go out on to the world markets and sell their goods in any way it considers best. That country is not involved in any combine or group such as GATT, and it can go out and sell whatever it likes at whatever price it wishes, and the people back home have to bear the brunt. That could never be done under our government, and I hope it never will.
There are many countries that are potential markets for Canadian goods. We will have to balance our trade books with the United States and attempt to direct some of that trade elsewhere. An illustration that comes to mind is Israel. We could do a considerable volume of business with Israel in citrus fruits. When I was in Israel last year I spoke to a German wholesale importer of fruits from Hamburg. He told me that the grapefruit produced in Israel today surpasses the fruit grown in the United States. Israel does not produce wheat or other feed grains for its animals in large volume and these commodities are readily available in Canada. I really believe we could do a good business with Israel today.
I also think we could obtain a greater proportion of our citrus fruits from the West Indies. Another market of which we are not taking full advantage is Spain. That country, I am sure, would buy our grain. Spain produces the finest oranges I have ever tasted. I point these out as examples of how we could direct our trade, not in the way the previous speaker outlined, but through normal

business channels and the trade service we maintain in those countries in an effort to obtain a greater share of that business for Canada.
In a year or so I hope world trade will be on an upswing. It appears to be contracting at the present time but I think this is a transitory condition and sincerely hope Canada will maintain and increase its markets in the countries of the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the previous speaker. On many points I agree with him but on others I do not. He referred at length to the part which wages play in the cost of Canadian production. All would agree that wages do play a large part in the cost of goods produced in Canada but in all fairness we must face the fact that wages are not the sole factor that serves to drive up the cost of Canadian production. Indeed we must take into account profits, taxes, plant and equipment, methods of production, transportation, plant efficiency and all the things which contribute to the cost of Canadian production.
If we are to face this problem I think we must recognize it is more than a matter of maintaining wages at their present level or reducing them. It is also a matter of being able to maintain or reduce expenditure in all the other fields that relate to Canadian production. I think we can sum up the whole thing by saying that what we need in Canada is greater productivity and I use the word "productivity" in its broadest scene.
I listened, as I have on many occasions during the last two or three years, to hon. members opposite make their recriminations of the previous administration. I suppose in politics that is fair game but I would suggest that the serious trade problems facing us now are not going to be solved by this government telling the country what the last government did not do. The position this government must now take is one of leadership. Hon. gentlemen opposite will solve nothing by becoming the critics of the critics. That will get no one anywhere.
I do agree with my hon. friend when he says we have to operate within our means. I believe that is the big problem that faces all of us at the present time. We in all branches of Canadian industry must learn to stand on our own feet as the hon. member says. We must not become too dependent on government.
As far as selling Canadian production is concerned I think we just have to get out and sell. We have heard a great deal in the last
Trade Balance
two or three years of the need to buy Canadian. This is not original on my part but I suggest it is equally important to sell Canadian.
We have a large imbalance of trade at the moment. I agree with the hon. gentleman who just resumed his seat that we should make an effort to balance our trading picture but it will be a very difficult task. For example, with respect to merchandise trade, next year we would either have to increase our exports by $400 million or decrease our imports by $400 million, or increase one and decrease the other by roughly $200 million. With respect to the total trade picture, the total balance of trade including merchandise and non-merchandise, next year we would either have to increase our exports by $1,500 million or decrease our imports by that amount or split it between the two. If we take into account that we are not too far from the time when we will lose $300 million in uranium exports, we have to realize that the figure is perhaps more accurately $2 billion.
A serious effort will have to be made to bring our trade balances more into line. We live in a country where trade is very important, a country where one out of three people depends for his livelihood on export trade. A country like Canada that is large in area with great natural resources and a small population necessarily depends on exporting a large percentage of its production. We are not in the same position as our neighbours to the south. That country is a third of the size of ours and has ten times our population. Its productivity is higher than ours. If it did not receive nearly as much export trade as it is now receiving, perhaps its economy would still carry on without undue fluctuation but that is not true with respect to the Canadian economy.
On other occasions inside and outside the house the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) has said there has been an increase in imports into Canada and an increase in exports from Canada. While it is a good thing that exports have increased and it is good that our imports increase to a certain extent, but not too much, the people who talk about these figures rarely explain the real relationship between them.
The unfortunate part about it is that during the past year our imports into this country have increased much more than our exports. Our merchandising trade imbalance in 1957 was $579 million; in 1958, it was $170 million; last year, it was $386 million. If we take our merchandising deficit due to the exchange of physical goods and the nonmerchandising deficit due to the payment of

Trade Balance
non-tangible services, our total deficit would be about $1,460 million. Of this amount, our merchandising trade deficit was roughly 25 per cent. In the year 1958 it was only 17 per cent. Our exports increased in 1959 by some 5 per cent, from $4,890 million to $5,152 million. Our imports increased in the same time by nine per cent, from $5,060 million to $5,538 million.
Over the years Canada has depended on an overseas surplus to offset the trade deficit with the United States. In the year 1959 there was a very distinct and a very disturbing change. Our total overseas deficit was $224 million, on top of a total deficit of $1,236 million with the United States of America. One of the most disturbing things about our overseas trade is our trade with the United Kingdom. Our surplus in 1956 was $252 million; in 1957, $138 million; in 1958, $108 million; and in 1959 only $52 million. Over these years we have seen our surplus with the United Kingdom decrease to only 20 per cent of what it was in 1956. With the remainder of the sterling area, the overseas countries, we have always had a fair balance. The surplus is now at an all time low of $12 million. It was $60 million in 1958. With the non-sterling area of western Europe in 1952 we had a surplus of $330 million; in 1959 this was converted into a deficit of $150 million.
With the rest of the world we had a record deficit of $137 million in 1958, and in 1959 it reached a new record of $139 million. It is very obvious that Canada is adding to her obligations at a faster rate than she is able to meet them. This is a most serious situation. It is partly due to the changes in production and trade throughout the world, particularly since the second world war, but it is also true that it is partly due to the policies of this government which in my view have been based on expediency rather than on sound trading principles.
Despite the bright hopes and promises of the present government two and a half years ago, it is clear that Canada is losing ground in its most important markets. Surely nobody in Canada today can look with anything but grave concern at the sharp reversal from a surplus to a deficit in trading with Europe. Of all Europe only Great Britain, as I said just now, made possible a surplus with Canada and even this was reduced by 50 per cent over last year.
The Prime Minister's hope of a 15 per cent diversion of trade has not worked out very well. The reverse has happened, and we are now buying more from the United States than we ever did before. I come from a province which is very dependent upon trade. Nearly

everything we use has to be brought into the province; in the main it is brought in from the mainland of Canada, something to the value of $250 million, and nearly everything we produce is sold outside the confines of Canada. I do not think it is unfair for my province to feel that since it provides such a worth-while domestic market for the produce of the Canadian mainland it can look to the federal government for policies which will preserve its export trade with the rest of the world.
I think we are entering into a period when we are beginning to experience the results of a renewal of the production and trade facilities of western Europe. They have not been able to measure up in those fields since the war as they did before, but now they are overcoming the effects of the very devastating war and they are producing materials which can be sold in markets where normally Canada has been able to sell in the last eight or ten years. We are being surrounded by trading blocs. We now have five large trading blocs composed of 38 countries and hundreds of millions of people. Certainly, these trading blocs will change the trading picture as we knew it in Canada heretofore. The only thing which Canada can do is to find out what changes are taking place and endeavour to meet those changes in a sound and sensible manner.
I give you one example. There are proposed tariffs for the European common market and they are outlined on page 28 of the March 12 issue of the Financial Post. One that concerns me very much is this:
Salt cod: Italy was the one good market in the common market area, and we had negotiated an agreement with Italy for free entry.
Now the common tariff is set at 12 per cent-18 per cent.
Canadian exports will suffer unless the Italian tariff can be negotiated downwards this fall.
If this tariff is not negotiated downwards, certainly it is going to have a tremendous effect on one of the main exports from my province.
Besides these trading blocs we, too, have to face the fact that we have the Russian trade giant who is gradually looking over the remainder of the world for markets where he can send his own produce produced under state control and sold by state trade. Here in Canada, of course, there is nothing in the form of state trade and it will be very difficult for a country like Canada to compete with a country which sells produce by state trade.
We have, for example, figures of the government of the Netherlands showing the amount of wheat sold through Rotterdam in 1958 and 1959. In 1958 Canada sold 485 million bushels and in 1959 the figure was

152 million bushels. The United States sold 262 million bushels in 1958 and 272 million bushels in 1959. But while the Soviet union only sold 8 million bushels through Rotterdam in 1958, in 1959 that country sold 308 million bushels.
Here is an example of what is happening with respect to wheat as far as Russia is concerned. One begins to wonder what will come next. Will it be the pulp and paper industry, will it be the fishing industry or will it be any of the other industries upon which the economy of Canada is founded? Far from being complacent about that problem, which was the immediate problem of the moment, we took very quick action. Trade has been one of the main preoccupations of the government. One of the first
