speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the break for the supper hour I was dealing by way of introduction with certain comments made by the Leader of the Opposition, who was accusing me of complacency and too great optimism, and I had indicated that I was not alone in taking an optimistic point of view with regard to Canada's position. I had read rather hurriedly the various articles in the Financial Post dealing with the provinces, showing that in the provinces right across this country there is a feeling of optimism. I started off with Nova Scotia, which by chance happened to be the page I turned to first, and I had got as far as the situation in Manitoba.
Then I notice that similar optimistic points of view are shown in the other western provinces-in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia-where they all point, first, to the fact that 1959 was a good year and, second, that the prospect for advancement in 1960 is excellent. In each of those three provinces you get a story of capital investment in industry, whether it is in manufacturing or in the resource industries, which will lead, as the premiers say, toward greater prosperity for their provinces.
A similar story of optimism comes from Newfoundland and from Prince Edward Island, the one province which lacks some of the resources with which the other provinces are favoured. But, nevertheless, there there is a feeling and an expression of opinion that times are good and that there is no need to be pessimistic about the future. So I make no excuse whatsoever for taking an optimistic view of Canada's future during this decade of the sixties.
During the course of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition he dealt at some length with Canada's foreign indebtedness, and I will have occasion to point out some errors in the use of language by the Leader of the Opposition, who is generally quite careful and precise in his use of language. When he was summing up his speech he talked about a record deficit in Canada's total trade, which is an inaccuracy. He talked about current transactions, which include trade plus the invisible items or the non-merchandise items. Similarly he talked about the deficit in, as he put it, our trade with the United States when he should have said our current transactions with the United States so that you can separate out from that the so-called invisible items, the non-merchandise items, and then deal with the commodity items or the actual trade items.

Trade Balance
When you are talking about Canada's foreign indebtedness I think it is important that the increase which has occurred in the post-war period should be seen in its proper perspective. In the first place, as foreign investment in Canada rose, so did Canadian investment abroad. Between 1945 and 1959 Canada's gross foreign liabilities increased from $8 billion to $24 billion and Canadian gross assets abroad rose from $4 billion to $8.6 billion. Thus Canadian net foreign indebtedness-that is, the gross liabilities less the gross assets-amounted to $15.4 billion in 1959 or 44 per cent of Canada's gross national product in that year.
I think it is important to relate these figures of foreign indebtedness to the productive capacity of a country as measured by its gross national product. When the war came to an end in 1945 Canada had been able to reduce some of her foreign indebtedness, and her net international indebtedness amounted to $4 billion or 34 per cent of the gross national product. This compares with a net international indebtedness of $5.5 billion in 1939, which was 98 per cent of the gross national product in that year. This means that the present ratio of Canada's net foreign indebtedness to our ability to support such an indebtedness, and that is reflected in the total value of goods and services produced, is currently less than half of what it was before the war, namely 44 per cent compared with 98 per cent.
The point, then, is that while foreign investment has been growing in Canada in the post-war period in absolute terms, the rate of the economic expansion of this country has been even more rapid, surpassing the rate of increase in Canadian foreign indebtedness.
It is also true that foreign debt service charges have risen in absolute terms in the post-war period. Interest and dividends paid to non-residents rose from $312 million in 1946 to $656 million in 1959 or by 110 per cent. During the same period interest and dividend payments received by Canadians from their foreign investments rose from $70 million to $170 million or by 143 per cent. Since receipts have risen more rapidly than amounts paid out, the net relative burden of interest and dividend payments on the economy has declined.
You can illustrate that by the following figures. The ratio of net interest and dividend payments to the gross national product amounted to 1.4 per cent in 1959, 2 per cent in 1946, 4.4 per cent in 1939, and 5 per cent in 1930; and going back as far as the beginning of the twentieth century the ratio is 3 per cent. These figures illustrate that the rapidly expanding Canadian economy has been able

to take a significant accumulation of foreign investment in its stride and that the burden of carrying interest and dividend payments to foreign investors has declined fairly consistently over the life of the last two generations. I think that is helpful, Mr. Speaker, in getting this foreign indebtedness into its proper perspective in relation to the strength of the economy of Canada.
With nations as with individuals and businesses the justification for borrowing can be judged only in relation to capability for carrying the debt and on the basis of how the resources are being used. The Leader of the Opposition attempted to leave the impression that Canada is incurring an increasingly onerous and excessive burden of debt.
Canada's deficit on current international transactions reached $1,460 millions in 1959. Considered in absolute terms, this is the highest deficit Canada has so far experienced. It is also true that the size and wealth producing capacity of the Canadian economy is greater than it has ever been before. So I repeat that a proper assessment of this deficit requires that it be considered in relation to the growth of the economy as a whole and, more particularly, in relation to the foreign earning capacity of the economy.
While Canada's current deficit increased by $36 million between 1957 and 1959, Canada's current earnings from international transactions in the same period increased by $227 million, that is, from $6,530 million to $6,757 million. As a proportion of Canada's total earnings the deficit in 1959 remains about the same as in 1957 and the present deficit in relation to our exports is far less than in earlier periods of rapid development in the Canadian economy. At the end of 1959, Canada's net foreign indebtedness had risen to $15.4 billion. This figure is well below one half of the annual gross national product whereas in 1926 our net foreign indebtedness was equal to the gross national product. Consequently, I say that our debt, considered in relation to our wealth producing capacity, is far less of a burden now than it was in the past.
Hon. members may say: have Canadians as a nation been wasteful in the use of resources while borrowing large amounts from abroad during the last five years? They may ask: has this additional foreign borrowing been used to support unwarranted levels of consumption? I think the Leader of the Opposition was attempting to give that impression. During the five-year period between 1955 and 1959, the growth of personal consumption in Canada has been little more than the growth in domestic production-24 per

cent as compared with 22 per cent-and during the five-year period total consumer outlays as a proportion of the total resources available within the economy have declined slightly from the level of the preceding five-year period when deficits were small and non-existent.
On the other hand, total capital outlays in the 1955-59 period as a proportion of total resources available have increased significantly. During this period capital expenditure in Canada exceeded one quarter of the gross national product, a substantially higher proportion than that of any other major trading nation.
These comparisons suggest that the additional resources obtained from abroad have been put to constructive purposes. The physical evidence of this is everywhere about us. From 1954 to 1959 Canada's electric generating capacity was increased by one-half, aluminum by one half, basic steel by nearly two-fifths, asbestos and copper by one-third, nickel mining by one quarter, pulp and newsprint by one quarter and petroleum refining by nearly 60 per cent. Oil pipe line mileage nearly doubled, while natural gas gathering and transmission lines tripled. The production of petroleum nearly doubled, while the output of natural gas and iron ore tripled. Chemical products increased by more than one quarter.
In short, this was a period not only of major expansion but also of the diversification of Canadian industry. In the last two years Canada has constructed two thirds of a million housing units, 50 per cent more than in the preceding five years. In the same period expenditures on new hospital facilities increased by one half, on schools by two thirds and on universities threefold. Twice as much was spent on roads. Taking into account all these factors, the size of Canada's deficit in relation to the foreign earning capacity, the size of the debt in relation to productive capacity and the trend of consumption and investment in relation to total resources there is little in this picture to substantiate the claim that Canadians have been living beyond their means.
There are differences of view as to the extent to which we should resort to borrowing from abroad and how the resources available might best be used. One course-and I do not know whether the Leader of the Opposition wants us to adopt this or not; he seemed to suggest it and then rather to withdraw-would be to maintain the pace of development by increasing domestic savings at the expense of current consumption, thereby reducing our reliance on borrowings from abroad. This would require a high degree
Trade Balance
of voluntary self-restraint, some change in the incentives conditioning spending or some form of enforced austerity imposed on the Canadian public or a combination of these.
Another course which has been proposed would involve limiting the rate of spending, including capital outlay, to a level which could be sustained without foreign borrowing. This would mean taking a decision as to what expenditures should be curtailed. Should Canadians be denied comfortable homes? With the school age population increasing more rapidly than the total population, should we build fewer schools? Should we spend less on highways and streets in the face of growing traffic problems? These are some of the questions which arise in relation to this suggestion. Is resource development proceeding too rapidly? Should we curtail the development of iron ore and base metal resources and other mineral products and thereby encourage the major foreign users to go elsewhere for sources of supply to meet their expanding requirements? Should we slow down the trend toward self-sufficiency in fuel?
These are difficult questions to answer. The real issue here is whether the present course of our development is sufficiently at variance with the interests of Canadians at large to warrant strong interference and control on the part of the government. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) was suggesting a great deal in the way of such control and interference.
I think it is important to bear in mind that the present course of development reflects the judgment of all Canadians, individually and in groups, acting each within their respective areas of responsibility within the context of a free marketing system. The tremendous progress which has been made in Canada and which is still proceeding indicates that the course which has been followed is a sound one.
On this question of foreign investment and Canadian investment it is well to keep in mind that Canadian savings finance the major portion of investment in Canada. In the course of the speech by the Leader of the Opposition attention was focused upon foreign investment in this country. But a major portion is financed by Canadian savings. Total Canadian savings at home and abroad represent four fifths, that is 80 per cent of the total net capital formation in Canada in the 1950-55 period and about two thirds in the 1956-58 period. If Canadian savings abroad are subtracted, Canadian savings invested in Canada represented about two thirds of the total net capital formation during the 1950-55

Trade Balance
period and 56 per cent during the 1956-58 period when capital spending was at very high levels.
There are, of course, broad areas of the economy such as agriculture and what is called social capital, that is, government institutions and housing and so on, in which the non-resident investment is relatively insignificant. It has been estimated that the net stock of social capital, which is largely financed by Canadian funds, is not much smaller than the net stock of industrial capital, including that invested in agriculture.
The tendency of foreign investment, particularly the direct type of investment, to concentrate in certain sectors of Canadian industry has resulted in a sizeable proportion of the capital employed in these industries being owned by non-residents. Thus at the end of 1957 capital owned by non-residents accounted for the following proportions of the total capital employed in these Canadian industries: petroleum and natural gas, 64 per cent; mining and non-ferrous metals smelting, 56 per cent; manufacturing, 50 per cent. The preference shown by foreign investors for certain branches of the Canadian manufacturing industry is reflected in the proportions of non-resident-owned capital to total capital employed in these industries, as of the end of 1957: the rubber industry, 84 per cent; the auto and parts industry, 78 per cent; the electrical apparatus industry, 70 per cent; the chemical industry, 62 per cent; the pulp and paper industry, 53 per cent.
On the other hand, Canadian-owned capital is predominant in the case of railways, other utilities, merchandising and construction, and in certain branches of manufacturing. At the end of 1957 Canadian-owned capital comprised 70 per cent of the total capital employed by the railroads, and 85 per cent of the total of other utilities. In manufacturing, resident-owned capital accounted for 79 per cent of the total capital employed by the textile industry, 76 per cent of that used by the primary iron and steel industry, 73 per cent of the capital of the beverage industry, 60 per cent in the case of the agricultural machinery industry, and 53 per cent for the transportation equipment industry, excluding the automobile industry.
The total capital employed in the selected group of industries, manufacturing, mining and smelting, utilities, merchandising and construction, rose from $11.9 billion in 1939, to $37.2 billion at the end of 1957, a gain of 213 per cent. The Canadian-owned capital employed in these industries increased from $7.4 billion to $24.3 billion over the 1939-57 period, or by 228 per cent. As a result, the share of the capital employed by this group

of industries which was owned in Canada rose from 62 per cent in 1939 to 65 per cent in 1957.
In recent years Canadians have been investing substantial sums in those domestic industries in which foreign capital is predominant. Between 1954 and 1957, for example, the capital owned by Canadians rose by $607 million in the case of the petroleum and natural gas industry, from $996 million to $1.6 billion; by $439 million in the Canadian mining and smelting industry, from $814 million to $1J billion; and by $857 million in the manufacturing industry, from $4.4 billion to $5.3 billion. The rise in the investment of Canadian capital in the chemical manufacturing industry, $127 million, increased the Canadian-owned proportion of the total employed by the industry from 36 per cent at the end of 1954 to 38 per cent at the end of 1957. Canadian-owned capital in the pulp and paper industry rose from $699 million in 1954 to $771 million in 1957.
Additional investment by Canadians enabled the shares of Canadian-owned capital employed in the electrical apparatus and auto and parts industries to be maintained unchanged over the 1954 to 1957 period, 30 per cent for the electrical apparatus industry and 22 per cent for the auto and parts industry.
Facts and figures like that are essential when one is considering the capital investment in this country to avoid getting the distorted picture that unfortunately has been given to us which might lead some people to consider that the only capital in this country came from abroad. Such is not the case.
The Leader of the Opposition dwelt at some length on this problem and indicated that a record deficit of nearly $1.5 billion occurred in our total trade. I would correct that figure to read $1,460 million. That represents the current account deficit in 1959. It was made up of a deficit of $386 million on merchandise trade-that is the export picture

and a deficit of $1,074 million on non-merchandise trade or invisible items. The deficit on merchandise trade or exports of $386 million is higher than in 1958 when it was $170 million. That was a time when there was a contraction of world trade. It was, however, lower than in 1956 when it was $728 million-that is the figure the Leader of the Opposition was rather reluctant to give us this afternoon-and also lower than in 1957 when it was $579 million.
There has been a progressive decline in Canada's deficit on merchandise trade with the United States since 1956. I wish to quote

from the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada for 1946 where, at page 23, we find this statement:
Canada has had a deficit in her current account transactions with the United States in every year from 1926 to 1943. In 1944 and 1945 there were small surpluses caused by special wartime factors. The average deficit over this 20-year period was $165 millions a year and the largest deficits (for example $437 millions in 1929) occurred in years of peacetime prosperity. The only peacetime years in which there was an approach towards balance were years of unemployment, stagnation and low imports, such as 1933-36.
Unless some developments occur which would produce a major change in the character of our trading relationships with the United States, it will be normal for Canada to have a deficit in its current account balance of payments with the United States, and this deficit is likely to average higher in the future than it has in the past.
In a speech I made in the house in January and in one I made last November I drew attention to the fact that over a period of 60 years, examining the favourable balances and the deficits, if you extracted from that period the war years and the immediate postwar years which the Leader of the Opposition did not do this afternoon when he was quoting figures-those unusual intervals of export trade abroad to support the war effort-you find that in the majority of years Canada had a trading deficit. The years in which that deficit occurred happened to coincide with periods of very rapid expansion in Canada.
In the speech I made in November I posed a question to the economists, which the Leader of the Opposition raised again this afternoon, to determine whether or not having a trade balance represented prosperity in the country when we had a trade balance in the very difficult years from 1933 to 1936, as I just read from the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada for 1946. I know that economists differ but, that being the case, I think laymen are privileged to differ as well, and I am still unconvinced that a trade deficit which does not involve the country in restrictive measures is bad for the country. We have been having trade deficits over the last several years and Canada's economy has been moving rapidly ahead.
The question was raised by the Leader of the Opposition as to whether something serious might happen if some of the capital funds that have come into Canada recently should be removed, because in 1959 a somewhat larger proportion of the movement of capital funds into Canada was of a short term character. These short term movements are a particularly variable element in the total and a decline in the outflow of funds of that type would tend to reduce the premium on the Canadian dollar and thus assist Canadian producers competing in international markets. This would not inflict
Trade Balance
grave and serious injury suddenly on Canada, as the Leader of the Opposition attempted to point out. It would be self-corrective and the way in which things have gone along indicates that in a free enterprise society we have managed quite well. If controls are suggested why then you get into an entirely different situation.
I pointed out that the Leader of the Opposition incorrectly referred to our total current transactions as a record trade deficit, and I suggested that the figures should be separated.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the minister has now for the third time corrected my reference to total trade deficits. That expression I got from the dominion bureau of statistics quarterly issue, Canadian balance of international payments, which refers in paragraph one to paragraph five to merchandise trade and non-merchandise trade. If you add the two of them together you get the total trade.
That is not a point of order.

After that pleasant interlude I will go on and give some valuable information to the house in regard to Canada's trading position. Our policy has been to

expand exports in order to increase our foreign earnings and thus narrow the substantial deficit which we have been incurring in our current transactions with the rest of the world.
I am just as eager as anyone else to see the continuous growth and diversification of our exports, and I believe more can be done both by business and through the assistance of the government and its agencies to expand our sales; but I wonder whether it is correct to make exports the culprit of the piece, or to expect from our export industries more than they can fairly be asked to accomplish.
When the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) was speaking this afternoon he said that in order to correct the imbalance we would have to increase our exports by $200 million and our imports by $200 million, or if we were to correct the imbalance in the total current transactions we would have to enlarge our exports by about $2 billion a year. I do not think it can all be done by way of exports. Export earnings are but one of the many factors entering into our annual deficits and the part they play or can play should be seen in proper perspective.
In an expanding and developing economy such as our own it is natural that our savings should be supplemented by foreign borrowings and that a current account deficit should be incurred as a result of the additional resources made available through imports. There is no economic law that requires that exports should immediately and automatically rise to bridge the trade imbalance caused by additional imports. Over time exports of goods and services must be adequate to service the foreign debt assumed during the development phase and as well as to finance imports and other outward payments, and until we have reached the stage of a mature creditor country there is likely to be a continuation of capital inflows to help in the process.
I recall that in 1956, when Mr. Howe was dealing with this subject of Canada's trade and her foreign indebtedness, he thought that there would be a period of 20 to 25 years elapse before Canada came to such a position that she would be a mature creditor country. It is not correct to expect that in the short run exports should rise promptly to finance the additional imports and other payments occasioned by development needs. The exports of a country at any particular time are determined mainly by what it has available to sell, the prices at which such exports are available and, most important, the level of foreign demand. That is a factor that is not in the control of the exporting country.

To the extent that the continuation of the deficit gives rise to concern, exports have their role to play. The investment made in this country in the 1950's, in manufacturing as well as in our resource industries, has for the most part been wisely placed in relation to demands both foreign and domestic which are likely to be placed on the economy in the future; the new productive facilities which have been created, will better enable us to take advantage of the opportunities offered by expanding world demand. The new growth thus achieved should provide the means to an improved livelihood as well as the requisite earnings to meet our external financial commitments.
The Leader of the Opposition expressed some alarm over the fact that, as he suggested, there is stagnation in the volume of our traditional exports. One of the most important and interesting developments in Canadian trade over the last 30-odd years has been a change in the pattern of our trade. Had we not had the development in our resources industry and the development in our manufacturing industries that have taken place recently we would not now be in a position to compete actively in world trade and maintain our position as one of the great trading nations of the world.
I had occasion to look into this last November, and I spoke on this subject in the city of Winnipeg. This is what I said with regard to the changing pattern of Canada's export trade:
In the very early days the fur trade was dominant, succeeded by timber exports, then by agricultural produce. Now, in our period we find a gradual increase in products other than those derived from the forest and farm and a steady growth in the export of manufactured articles.
Then I looked back to the year 1927 and compared it with 1957 to see what the change had been in 30 years.
In 1927 the ten leading exports were wheat, newsprint, flour, planks and boards, wood pulp, fish, automobiles, meats, barley and cheese. Thirty years later in 1957 four of these products, namely, newsprint, wheat, planks and boards and wood pulp retained their position but the other six have been replaced by aluminum, nickel, copper, iron ore, petroleum and asbestos .. .
In that 30-year period the volume of our exports increased fourfold and the value from $1) billion to $43 billion. The rise in volume and value continues. There has been a shift in the 30-year period from the export of raw materials to processed materials. In 1927, 47 per cent of total exports consisted of raw materials; in 1957 the percentage had dropped to 31. Partly manufactured materials rose from 15 per cent to 32 per cent; and chiefly manufactured retained its position at 37 per cent.
We surely would not expect our traditional exports, if you want to go all the way back to the time when fur was the chief one, to maintain their position in this modern world

when so much emphasis has been placed on manufactured articles derived from the mineral wealth of the country. Consequently that change and shift in the pattern of our trade has continued and it has vastly improved the economy of Canada, all based on capital investment in these industries.
The Leader of the Opposition and others have attempted to create the impression that Canada is somehow or other losing out in world markets. This was the situation last year too. Yet we have retained our place as a leading exporter in the world and in 1958, as I mentioned before the supper hour, we maintained the record level of exports we had reached in 1957 and in 1959 we exceeded it. How you can deduce from that that Canada is losing out in world markets surprises me indeed.
In 1958 Canada's exports held firm, and that was in the face of a general decline in world trade. This was one of the amazing things in 1958. General world trade declined but Canada's exports held firm. In 1959 total world exports were barely back to the 1957 level while Canada's exports had increased by more than 5 per cent from the 1957 and 1958 figures. In other words, Canada's products considered as a whole had more than held their own in world markets, and this upward trend in our exports has been accelerated in recent months. In the three-month period ended in January Canada's exports were 17 per cent higher than in the corresponding period one year ago. This growth has not been reflected only in certain markets, it applies to all the major export areas. For this same three-month comparison exports to the United States are up by 18 per cent, to the United Kingdom by 15 per cent, to continental western Europe by 21 per cent, to Japan by 32 per cent and to all other countries by 9 per cent. That gives us a good start in the year 1960. Again, as I said before six o'clock, I wonder why the Leader of the Opposition made such an error in judgment as to select this period when things are going so well to launch an attack on Canada's trading policy.

Would the minister permit a question? If the figures are as he has indicated in regard to our increased exports, how does he explain that this year we have an overseas deficit instead of an overseas surplus?

speechtext:
I will come to that as I go along. I intend to cover the waterfront in this speech on trade. The Leader of the Opposition took an hour and a half and I want to do justice to his remarks and to the subject. I will cover all these things as I proceed.
Trade Balance
Economic activity in the United States, the United Kingdom and the other major industrial countries is moving steadily ahead. This will involve continued growth in the demand for industrial materials, particularly minerals and forest products which together make up nearly two thirds of Canada's total exports. Industrial material exports have increased by about 30 per cent during the past year and further improvements are indicated for such items as pulp and paper, iron ore, nickel, aluminum and other base metals, asbestos, petroleum and chemicals.
In the manufactured goods field substantial progress is being made despite intensive international competition. Canadian firms are now working on large foreign orders in such highly competitive fields as transport aircraft and heavy electrical apparatus. Opportunities for extending this type of business are good.
The statement is frequently made that we are pricing ourselves out of world markets. This deserves examination. Again I put this before the house. How can this allegation be reconciled with the fact that our export trade stands at the highest level ever known? This is occurring when our competitive position in world markets is to some extent hampered by the premium on the Canadian dollar in foreign exchange.
The great bulk of our foreign exchange earnings on merchandising account are from the sale of primary commodities in world markets. With non-ferrous metals and pulp and paper, as with wheat, sales are at world market prices and we must be and are meeting the competition of other producers. It may be true that the coincidence of advancing production costs and higher transportation costs in a commodity like lumber renders us from time to time less competitive in certain markets, for example, the United Kingdom and the continent, but at the present time the prospects of an increase in exports of lumber and wood products to the United Kingdom are more favourable than they have been for several years and this year we expect an upturn in that particular market.
It is difficult to entertain seriously the suggestion that we are pricing ourselves out of world markets where in the case of iron ore, for example, there is a heavy inflow of foreign investment to develop Canadian sources of supply for the investor, and this type of investment must surely be profitable to us since it is committing the investor to an interest in Canada as a source and it is creating new foreign exchange earning power for Canada.
At the same time I think it is essential that we should be careful that we take no steps that would bring us to a state where we

Trade Balance
would price ourselves out of the world market in this age when that world market is very competitive. There are some products, particularly manufactured products, which other countries produce more cheaply than is the case in Canada, but we cannot expect to be the leading exporter of all goods that move in international trade. Nevertheless, over 30 per cent of our exports are made up of chiefly manufactured articles, where we have products of interest in world markets, and important examples are newsprint electrical apparatus, beverages and agricultural equipment. There are a host of other manufactured articles which go to make up the total.
With imagination in marketing, with aggressive sales promotion and with determination to take advantage of market opportunities throughout the world, I am sure that the contribution made to our export earnings by manufactured products can be steadily increased. That is being done by enterprising Canadian businessmen this year. Now that restrictions on trade have been removed in so many countries our businessmen in the export trade and others who want to enter it are beginning to take active steps to recover the ground that they lost at the outbreak of the second world war.
I think sometimes we overlook the fact that for 20 years Canadian goods, either by reason of the war situation or by restrictions imposed by the dollar countries after the war, have been excluded from markets they formerly occupied. It is for this reason we have had difficulty in connection with exports to the United Kingdom, western Europe and the countries of the commonwealth. But now that these trade restrictions have been removed, the opportunities are there for Canadian business to take advantage of them.
A remarkable response to the entry of Canadian goods into the United Kingdom has taken place recently. You have read about it in the newspapers. Enterprising Canadian businessmen have invaded United Kingdom markets closed to them for many years and have made surprising sales. It is only a little over a year ago that the best example occurred of what happens when controls are removed. I suppose for almost 20 years Canadian salmon could not find its way into the United Kingdom market because of quota restrictions. When these quota restrictions were removed the entire Canadian salmon pack was purchased by United Kingdom importers and once again appeared in the United Kingdom market.
The reports we are getting with regard to our commodity trade are encouraging. The foreign demand has given rise to an increase in the production of aluminum and nickel

and in copper has sustained capacity production. Active demand has reappeared for zinc and the forecast high level of United States steel production promises we will do better in 1960 than in 1959 in iron ore. In the forest products field the high levels established in 1959 may be exceeded in 1960 for newprint and woodpulp. I mentioned lumber to the United Kingdom market. The January bookings of business in lumber in that market were up almost 100 per cent over the previous year's levels. In chemicals Canadian exports are reaching new peaks. Early indications are that foreign sales of synthetic resins will reach a new all-time high in 1960, particularly benefitting from trade liberalization in various countries.
With our increased production facilities for fertilizers the prospects are that exports will increase by some 10 or 15 per cent, the major market for this product being the United States. Our foreign sales of synthetic rubber will also move forward due to current high levels of demand. Our aircraft industry is making headway in the transition from military aircraft production into commercial aircraft and has successfully negotiated sales of turboprop freighters to United States commercial air lines. Negotiations are presently taking place for additional export orders on a world-wide basis. In the field of lighter aircraft, export demand has been maintained for both land and amphibious aircraft. Designed in Canada to meet Canadian requirements, these types of aircraft have a wide variety of applications such as agricultural pest control, aerial survey work and for transportation to inaccessible areas where aircraft landing facilities are limited. There has also been a considerable demand for this type of aircraft for search and rescue purposes.
The electronics industry has also been favoured by the acceptance of Canadian aircraft in foreign markets. In addition to the equipment normally included in these aircraft it has, independently supplied both navigational and direction finding equipment to foreign buyers. In the communications field important contracts have been negotiated for microwave equipment in Europe, Venezuela and Colombia. A Canadian company has obtained a substantial order for carrier telephone equipment. The electronic equipment industry has been successful in obtaining orders for a wide range of the electronic control mechanisms. Interest is keen in heavy engineering products and next year's exports will reflect the successses which were achieved in 1959 on tenders submitted for hydraulic turbines on two separate projects in the United States and another in New Zealand, and a Canadian firm has been

successful in competing for orders for heavy electrical equipment in Venezuela.
The promising possibilities are not limited to the primary materials and capital equipment fields. There has been an enthusiastic response to the liberalization of import restrictions in the United Kingdom during 1959. On the subject of getting into the United Kingdom market-and this will answer in part the question of the Leader of the Opposition-may I say that our imports from the United Kingdom in 1956 were 8.5 per cent of our total imports, or $476 million, and rose in 1959 to $589 million or 10.7 per cent. From the United Kingdom we have been receiving imports greater than was the case a few years ago, and with the dollars earned by the sale of United Kingdom goods in Canada they have been in a better position to purchase from us. Within the last three years the Canadian exports to the United Kingdom have increased from $726 million in 1957 to $794 million in 1959. For the month of January the exports from Canada to the United Kingdom increased in one month by an amount almost equal to the total increase for the previous 12 months. This gives you some idea of the expansion of Canada's trade, and the maintenance and increase of our trade with the United Kingdom.

I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if the minister would permit a question at this point. I have been trying to follow his argument that the easier condition of trade as a result of the removal of restrictions, presumably by overseas countries since restrictions were not mainly on the part of the United States, then does not that make the fact that there is in total trade a current deficit in 1959 with overseas countries of $224 million, the first deficit for a great number of years, all the more serious? Does not the whole argument he is making point up the seriousness of the situation, and if I am wrong in my deductions would he just explain the argument he is seeking to make? I have taken the figures from page 22 of the Bank of Canada report, or the dominion bureau of statistics quarterly, page 6, has the same figures.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am showing that our export trade is being maintained and extended. At the same time there has been a shift in the trading pattern and Canada has been bringing in from overseas countries more goods than she was earlier and bringing in fewer from the United States. Whereas a few years ago our total imports on the merchandise side from the United States were 73 per cent of our total imports, that has dropped now to 68 per cent. The shift has been to bringing in imports from the United Kingdom, from countries in Europe and from the commonwealth. Actually, with overseas countries we have a favourable balance of trade for 1959 to the amount of $132 million. It has not disappeared; the favourable balance is still there. That, taken against the unfavourable balance with the United States, has left us with an unfavourable merchandise account of $386 million, and that is the figure with which I am dealing in this discussion.
Along with the export of resource material, primary products, materials from resource industries and manufactured articles, there is another aspect of Canadian trade which I have mentioned before but which should be mentioned again, and that is the work which Canadian consulting engineers are doing abroad. They are the forerunners and experts of Canadian engineering progress. We have assisted the Canadian consulting engineers to the best of our ability in their work abroad, and I have nothing but commendation for the work which they are doing because as the consulting engineers move into countries like India, Pakistan, Norway or Sweden, or any country of the world, they tend to attract Canadian products to assist in the development of the projects which they have been undertaking. Canadian industry has generally been responsive to the new opportunities which are opening up in this decade for trade abroad.

Trade Balance
One might ask, what are we as a government doing about it? We are giving every possible assistance. We have a foreign trade service in the department which constantly keeps in touch with opportunities abroad and informs the department here, and through the department businessmen in Canada, of trading opportunities which they may be interested in. Right at this stage, because of the change that has resulted in the United Kingdom through the removal of restrictions, several of our commodity experts, experts in the consumer goods line, will be going to the United Kingdom for short periods to gather information at first hand which they will then relay to Canadian exporters here at home, and they will assist in staffing our commercial offices in the United Kingdom. We intend to assign in the near future a second timber specialist to work in the United Kingdom, and he will be located in the newly opened Glasgow office and will concentrate on trade work in the northern and western sectors of that market.
The department has been experimenting with new techniques for promoting exports of semi-processed materials, and this is in keeping with the objective of this government that Canadian raw materials should be further processed within the country.
The potentialities of a large number of large and small wood manufacturing plants have been surveyed and their range of product classified according to possible industrial applications. The information developed is in the hands of our office in London who search out market potentialities. Little has been done in the past to develop exports of component part manufactures, such as the automobile part makers. A similar approach will be made by officials of this department in this field to see what can be done to follow on established successes of one or two firms in finding markets in secondary industry in other countries, including the United States, for their products.
With regard to the trade commissioner service, I have mentioned this before in the house but it is worth repeating. We have now more than 100 trained and competent officers stationed at 60 posts in 46 different countries. We have recently opened a new post at Glasgow. Two more new posts will be opened in 1960, one in Australia and the other at Lagos, and further new offices will be opened where it appears that there will be opportunities for Canadian business to develop. From all indications we expect that the year 1960 will be a record year for Canadian trade.
Mr. Speaker, the question of Canada's trade policy arises and there seems to be

some misunderstanding with regard to it. There is no misunderstanding in the minds of the government. We know exactly what we want done and how to go about it; and as I mentioned before the supper hour Canada's trade has been a priority engagement of ours since we took office and we have taken great steps toward maintaining that trade and expanding it, and we will continue along that line.
Canada continues to follow a trade policy which is directed to the achievement of a trading system in which Canadian exports have access to markets throughout the world on a basis of equality with all other suppliers. The structure of Canada's trade does not permit a neat bilateral balance between Canada and each of her trading partners. We hope that where there is a trading deficit with one trading partner, that will be made up by a trading surplus with another. We believe that it is to the best advantage of Canada to support a multilateral international trading system based on the principles of most favoured nation tariff treatment and non-discrimination. Trade agreements which incorporate these principles have been concluded with all the major trading nations of the world, particularly through the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Under the agreed international rules of the GATT and of the IMF substantial progress has been made in expanding Canadian export opportunities and in ensuring Canadian exporters equal treatment in world markets.
As regards tariff barriers to trade, Canada's access to foreign markets has been markedly expanded through the reduction and binding against increases on a wide range of tariffs of interest to Canada. Canada has declared its intention to participate in a further general tariff conference called for September of this year. Moreover, during the past two years and particularly during the year 1959 the United Kingdom and other countries of western Europe have made major progress in accordance with their international obligations in dismantling quantitative restrictions against Canadian trade. At the present time, Canadian exports enjoy generally unrestricted access to these markets. While Canadian exporters continue to be faced with import controls in their access to many of the less developed markets, the discrimination which has been made against dollar suppliers has been all but eliminated.
We are continuing to press strongly for the removal of the few remaining discriminations with regard to our exports to the United States market. Some 80 per cent of Canada's trade now enters free of duty or at rates of less than 10 per cent, and Canadian shipments to that market are at a record level. The

quantitative restriction on the sale of Canadian petroleum in the United States market has been removed. Apart from the quotas maintained by the United States on imports of lead and zinc, no new barriers have been placed in the way of Canadian trade, and the opportunities for export to the United States market are greater now than at any time in the past. We look forward to securing even greater access to the United States market in the course of the forthcoming round of multilateral tariff negotiations.
At the same time, vigorous efforts are being made to strengthen Canada's relation with its commonwealth partners. A trade agreement was signed recently with Canberra providing for improved trading opportunities between Canada and Australia and this agreement further expands Canada's opportunities in that market. Steps are now under way looking to the strengthening of Canada's trade relations with the West Indies. The 1958 Montreal conference contributed substantially to the improvement of mutual understanding among the commonwealth countries. As regards the development of European regional arrangements, Canada's trade policy is directed toward the production and establishment of a beneficial trading interest in that area and to secure advantages from the new trading opportunities which closer economic integration in Europe may provide. To this end Canada has at every opportunity impressed upon the participating European countries the importance of avoiding the emergence of any new barriers against Canadian trade and of developing outward-looking arrangements which would lead to the expansion of international trade rather than to its contraction.
Canada has welcomed the opportunity to participate more actively in the discussions now taking place in Europe as a further means of expanding world trade and of promoting Canadian interests both in Europe and in other parts of the world. At the Paris economic meetings in January, which were attended by the Minister of Finance and myself, important decisions were taken looking toward Canadian and United States participation with the European countries in a revised organization for economic co-operation. A trade committee was established which will have its first meeting at the end of March. Through these meetings, and through the GATT and in our direct contacts with our trading partners, the government has taken the necessary steps to further our important export interests.
New challenges and problems are arising as we enter the decade of the sixties. We intend to keep our economy and our external policies in a healthy state to meet them.

Those are the ways in which we are approaching this important problem of Canada's trade. There is no aspect of it which is not receiving our attention. We are prepared to attend, and we have attended, these international meetings at which trade problems have been discussed, and Canada's interest has been put forward with emphasis and vigour at those meetings. We have urged countries which are forming regional trading blocs to be careful not to interfere, first of all, with their obligations under GATT and secondly with their trading relations with countries outside their regional blocs.
Fear is sometimes expressed with regard to the change in the trading pattern resulting from the formation of the common market in Europe, the outer seven, or the new organization formed among the Latin American republics. I have not shared some of the alarm which has been expressed. At the same time I think we have to be on the alert to see that these trading arrangements do not hamper and restrict world trade. I look at it this way, that western Europe is one of the great trading areas of the world; western Europe is not self-sufficient; it has to trade with other people. Just to show that it is not self-sufficient, may I draw the attention of the house to a report in the Globe and Mail of March 18 where the Netherlands ambassador to Canada was talking about these two groups. He said, and I quote from this article:
Exports of the six common market countries in 1958 remained 30 per cent within their own orbit. They went to the extent of 22 per cent to the countries of the outer seven, and 48 per cent found their way to the rest of the world.
In the case of the outer seven, 17 per cent of their combined exports remained within the group; 22 per cent went to the common market and 61 per cent to the rest of the world.
Then the ambassador went on to say:
The trade interest of the European groups in the outside world is important enough to warrant the expectation that no policies will be pursued which would seriously jeopardize these vitally needed markets.
Europe takes things from us, too. Of Canada's total exports for 1958, 8.7 per cent went to the common market countries, about one third of this being agricultural products. Of that, 65 per cent was represented by wheat. In the same year, 4.7 per cent of Canada's imports came from the common market countries. Then, of course, we do a greater business still with the countries of the outer seven, because the outer seven contains the United Kingdom. Our trade with western Europe is a substantial proportion of our external trade. Western Europe will require things from Canada in the future just as in the past, and as the standard of

the United Kingdom also dismantled practically all of their restrictions during 1959. In addition there were minor liberalization moves in Pakistan, South Africa and Ghana. In the West Indies there were two major steps toward liberalization of imports and in the light of these developments it was decided to terminate the West Indies trade liberalization plan which was originally established in 1951 in order to provide access to the West Indies for Canadian goods which otherwise would have been completely excluded. As controls were removed the scope of the plan was progressively reduced and by September, 1959 most Canadian exports were entering the West Indies without restriction. As a result of that, Canada agreed with the United Kingdom and the West Indies to terminate the liberalization plan effective December 31, 1959 and has received assurance that the West Indies will consult Canada about licensing arrangements for products covered by the plan which were not yet liberalized on the understanding that access generally to West Indies markets for Canadian exports of these products would be on terms no less favourable than in the past.
Discussions continued during 1959 between the various West Indian territories regarding the establishment of a customs union in the new federation. These developments were followed closely. As agreed at the Montreal conference the revision of the Canada-West Indies trade agreement of 1926 will be dependent on the progress which the federation makes toward a customs union.
The new Canada-Australia trade agreement which was negotiated in 1959 in Canberra was signed on February 12, 1960 and will come into force when ratified by the two governments. We will be discussing that in this house later on in the spring.
The agreement provides increased safeguards and improved access for Canadian exporters to Australia. In addition to receiving British preferential tariff treatment on most products Canada will be accorded some important new concessions. Australia has undertaken to bind against an increase in the actual rates of duty on a number of products of interest to Canada including canned salmon and sardines, sausage casings, knitting machine needles, office machinery, some chemicals, paper makers' felts, and asbestos. Australia will bind the existing margins of preference on most products of interest to Canada. The new agreement also contains provisions relating to the suspension of margins of preference in Australia through administrative action, the use by both countries of anti-dumping duties and the establishment of machinery for consultation of trade and economic matters.

During 1959 the proposals agreed upon at the Montreal conference for co-ordinating the existing arrangements for consultation and co-operation among members of the commonwealth were implemented with the holding of the first meetings of the commonwealth consultative economic council. The council met at the senior official level in London from May 5 to 8. A meeting of the council at the ministerial level took place on September 23 and 24, also in London. In addition, a meeting of the Canada-United Kingdom continuing committee was held on July 2 and 3 in order to provide an opportunity for discussing matters of particular interest in the relations between those two countries, and representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce were present at all those meetings.
Now with regard to the United Kingdom membership in the European free trade association, Canada naturally has a great interest in this because the United Kingdom is our best customer in western Europe; but we do not foresee any great change in our trading relations with the United Kingdom, despite their connection with this group called the outer seven. Canada will continue to receive free entry of most of its exports to the United Kingdom.
Although in general the European free trade association does not involve the elimination of internal tariffs on agricultural and fishery products it does contain provision for negotiation of special arrangements concerning trade in agricultural products between member countries. Under an arrangement of this kind with Denmark the United Kingdom has undertaken to reduce its tariffs on Danish bacon and canned pork luncheon meat by 50 per cent on January 1, 1960, and eliminate it altogether on July 1, 1961. Then the United Kingdom has agreed to a request by Norway that frozen fish fillets should be treated as an industrial product and the tariff removed over a 10-year period. In the light of the proposal to eliminate Canada's preference in the United Kingdom because of this arrangement with Denmark, Canada made representations to the United Kingdom for the removal of the import restrictions which have been maintained on Canadian bacon for balance of payments purposes and the United Kingdom agreed to establish a quota of 25,000 tons of frozen pork from the dollar area for the year beginning January 1, 1960. This will give you an idea of the careful attention that is paid to trading arrangements entered into by our trading partners and the adjustments that have to be made in order that trade may be maintained.
The resumption of economic expansion in the United Kingdom appeared to lag behind

Trade Balance
that in the United States and, to a lesser extent, behind that of the major industrial countries of western Europe. In consequence, the effect of this recovery on the level of Canadian exports was relatively slight during the year as a whole-an increase of 2.1 per cent. Toward the end of 1959, however, British demand strengthened and in the last quarter of the year Canadian exports reached a record level for the period. Many of Canada's major agricultural and industrial exports to the United Kingdom remained about stable between 1958 and 1959. Wheat and flour, flaxseed, woodpulp, pulpwood, aluminum, copper and lead remained virtually unchanged in export value in the two years.
Among the more notable changes taking place, exports of uranium ores rose from $13,500,000 in 1958 to $33 million in 1959. Sales of oilcake and meal rose from $6 million to $15 million, and for the first time in many years Canada shipped a sizeable quantity of butter to the United Kingdom, valued at $6 million. Iron ore, newsprint, paper, tobacco and zinc advanced more moderately. There was some decline in value of our exports to the United Kingdom of barley, canned fish, lumber, nickel, platinum and abrasives. Purchases from the United Kingdom increased more markedly, rising by over 13 per cent in 1959 from the level established in 1958, a dollar increase of $70 million. This was highly concentrated in larger sales to Canada of automobiles and parts and other consumer durables and semidurables.
In January, 1960, Canada's exports to the United Kingdom were $13,500,000 higher than in the same month of 1959, an increase of almost one quarter. This compares with a rise of $16.1 million in sales to the United Kingdom in the year 1959 as a whole over the figure for 1958.
With improvement in the general level of prices for raw materials and agricultural products, the basic export commodities of other commonwealth countries, foreign exchange difficulties eased for most of these countries in 1959. While for the year as a whole Canadian exports to this area to those other commonwealth countries were slightly below those of 1958, they showed marked gains of 9 per cent and 13 per cent in the third and fourth quarters respectively. Exports of wheat to India were $22 million lower than in 1958, when large shipments were made under long term credit and aid arrangements to help meet the shortage situation prevailing at that time. On the other hand, South Africa was back in the market for wheat in 1959, purchasing $15,500,000 worth as against none in 1958. Wheat sales

were up to Pakistan and Ghana. Australia and South Africa purchased substantially more newsprint paper in 1959. Sales of automobiles and parts to Australia were greater in 1959, as were those of aluminum to South Africa. The general improvement in the price of bulk commodities which these countries supply to Canada-wool, tea, sugar, bauxite and rubber-was the main factor in the 12 per cent increase in Canadian purchases of these goods in 1959.
That, Mr. Speaker, gives you some idea of Canada's trade relations with commonwealth countries. Our trade is being maintained with those countries and is being expanded. Great efforts are being made through our trade commissioners abroad, and through the activities of Canadian businessmen, to enlarge Canada's trade with commonwealth countries. We have a long history of excellent trade with all of those commonwealth countries and we are going to make every effort to maintain it at a very high level. The opportunities now have been greatly widened for Canadian exporters, owing to the removal of restrictions that were imposed by those countries for reasons very largely beyond their control.
But with the general world recovery taking place we are now seeing the effects of the liberalization of trade, and I have listed tonight a great many of the articles of interest to Canada that now can be sold freely in the United Kingdom, in Australia and in other countries of the commonwealth. This is one of the reasons, among many others, why we are looking forward to a banner year in 1960; one of the reasons why in the year-end report of the Department of Trade and Commerce the view was expressed that our export position would improve and that gradually the gap between exports and imports would narrow.
We have based our forecast for 1960 on very sound grounds; it is not a blind, optimistic survey without relation to facts. The facts are evident, and I have drawn attention to them tonight. It surely follows that if markets that were closed to goods from Canada for 20 years are now open, there is a great opportunity for Canadian exports. It surely follows from experience that if some of our Canadian exporters have already enjoyed an expansion in the United Kingdom market that that opportunity can be expanded and seized by other exporters from Canada. These are reasons why we are not depressed over the Canadian trade picture at all. In fact, there is reason for confidence in the future. Canada has the resources. These markets are now open to us and yet,

during the last three years before these markets were open to us, we were maintaining our position among the great world traders.
In the year 1960 the figures for the early part of the year indicate a very important and substantial improvement in our export trade. Therefore the people who have been expressing some fear and alarm with regard to the deficit that we experienced in our merchandise balance for the year 1959 may take heart. It will not take much in the way of exports to close that gap, which was much higher in the year 1956. It was double what it was for 1959. So our trade picture, far from being a depressing one, is an encouraging one.
The Leader of the Opposition dwelt at some length on the development of the regional trading blocs in western Europe, which I mentioned casually a few minutes ago, and expressed alarm that these trading blocs might do damage to Canada's trade, and I suggested that in the long run Canada's trade with western Europe would likely be improved rather than restricted. These European trading arrangements deserve the most careful attention and we have been giving to these trading blocs just that type of attention. We have been watching them very closely. Right from the very beginning or at least from the time that we took office in 1957, in speaking at GATT conferences and other conferences we urged that these new trading arrangements in Europe should be made outward-looking rather than restrictive. We urged that no tariff barriers should be raised against trade. We urged that these western European nations should observe their obligations under GATT and we particularly stressed the importance of maintaining for Canada in these markets our position in agricultural products.
We know the importance of the markets in the United Kingdom and Western Europe for our Canadian wheat. That is where most of it is sold and of course it is of vital importance to us that that market be maintained. So there is every reason for Canadians to view these developments in western Europe and watch them with the greatest of care. The government has been doing that and Canadian officials have kept a very close eye on the situation and have kept us very well informed with regard to these matters.
The European economic community consists of six nations, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. It has a population of 160 million people. Their aim is to create an economic community with free trade within the area and a common tariff and common economic policies toward the outside world. The treaty calls for the implementation of these arrangements over a period of some 12 years.
Trade Balance
On January 1, 1959, the first steps in the elimination of tariffs within the Six were taken with a reduction of 10 per cent in the rates of duty on trade within the area and by an increase of 20 per cent in the quotas maintained by the member countries on each other's trade. In order to reduce the extent of tariff differentiation which this move would inevitably involve at this stage some of these reductions were extended to Canada and to other countries on a most favoured nation basis. This applied in particular with respect to the tariffs now in force in France and Italy. The next stage in the reduction of tariff barriers within the area is scheduled to take place on July 1, 1960.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the speeding up of the program of the Six toward economic unity which is their desired goal. Let us consider what is the effect on Canada or what might be the effect on Canada. Among the major issues faced by the countries of the European economic community during 1959 was the special problem of working out the level of the common tariff to be established for a number of important items. These included the rates on a number of products of particular importance to Canada such as aluminum, lead and zinc, synthetic rubber, timber and wood pulp. These negotiations are now complete and their implications are being studied.
While these discussions were going on Canada took every opportunity to urge the member countries of the economic community to establish rates of duty on these important items of Canadian trade at levels which would not prevent the continuation and further development of Canadian trade. While that was going on with regard to these six countries, seven countries consisting of the United Kingdom, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal initiated negotiations among themselves looking toward a free trade area. They signed their convention on November 20 and expect to have it ratified by the governments of the member countries by the end of March of this year. They are looking toward the progressive achievement of free trade among the seven countries through the removal of tariffs and other trade barriers over a period of 10 years.
The first 20 per cent cut among the members is to take place on July 1 of this year, and unlike the European economic community the free trade association does not provide for a common tariff against outside countries. Each country will be free to maintain and to alter its own tariffs and to pursue a generally independent commercial policy.
The seven countries are all low tariff countries. One of the declared objectives of

Trade Balance
the Seven in forming a free trade association is to facilitate the early establishment of an association for the removal of trade barriers and the promotion of closer economic cooperation with the countries of the European economic community. The Seven have been pressing for a Europe-wide free trade area.
With regard to our trade with western Europe I will just give a few of the articles that Canada ships to western Europe and the amounts. One of the reasons for the decline in our total trade with western Europe in 1959 was that we had previously sold many military aircraft to Belgium and West Germany. Aircraft to the value of $85 million were sold to these countries and that, of course, was not repeated. That was part of a NATO commitment. There was some reduction in our exports of wheat and copper to the Netherlands in 1959. Other than these items our exports to western Europe remained steady or improved.
Aluminum sales to France, West Germany and Italy were substantially above the 1958 values. Iron ore exports to the Netherlands were almost double. Flaxseed exports to West Germany and rapeseed exports to Italy' strengthened in 1959. Asbestos and primary iron and steel showed more moderate gains.
There were few marked changes in the commodity pattern of Canada's exports to the continental members of the European free trade area, exclusive of the United Kingdom. Sales of wheat were down, with a larger proportion of the imports of these countries being supplied from other European sources. On the other hand, shipments of aluminum and nickel were up. Outside of these items commodity exports were stable. On the import side, purchases from western Europe as a whole increased. This increase was largely in passenger automobiles and parts from West Germany, France and Italy.
I cannot give all the items of the trade that goes on between Canada and these countries of western Europe but I have given some indication of the importance of that trade to us and some indication of Canada's interest in making sure that these two new regional groupings in western Europe will keep as their objective the enlarging of trade and not the restricting of trade.
I continue to hope that they will maintain their interest in world trade. I mentioned earlier this year that I had had the privilege of seeing the ministers of commerce in most of these countries of the Six and the Seven, and each one assured me that his country, just as ours, was anxious to increase trade rather than restrict it.
We have one trading partner that outranks in size of the business that which we do in trade with all others combined and, of course,

that is the United States. The United States has been Canada's best customer back for a great many years and, alternately, Canada has been the United States' best customer. Our trade relations with the United States are of the greatest importance to our country. Canada's exports to the United States reached a record level of over $3 billion in 1959 and the trend has continued into 1960. The United States continues to be, by far, Canada's largest market and to supply the biggest share of Canada's import requirements. While the trade imbalance increased substantially early in 1959, this trend was reversed in the last quarter with a notable increase in Canada's exports to the United States.
Nineteen fifty nine was marked by a further improvement in Canada-United States trade relations. There was an increasing degree of co-operation between Canada and the United States in furthering our mutual trade objectives. In this connection, United States leadership in pressing for a relaxation of restrictions and the elimination of discrimination maintained for balance of payments reasons by many other countries was particularly welcome. Canada has also welcomed the more active United States participation in discussions relating to the development of regional trading arrangements in Europe.
Early in 1959 the joint United States-Canada committee on trade and economic affairs met in Ottawa. This committee, composed of cabinet ministers of the two countries, reviewed developments in the world economic and commercial situations and examined various issues bearing on trade and economic relations between Canada and the United States. A closer understanding and appreciation of the interests of the two countries was reached and there were useful discussions on matters of common interest. The Canadian side expressed concern over United States restrictions maintained on imports of lead, zinc and petroleum. Fruitful discussions were held regarding the problems for Canada arising out of the United States program for surplus disposal of agricultural products. It was agreed that these trade matters should be kept under continuing review in an effort to reach an equitable solution. Arrangements were made for quarterly meetings of wheat experts from the two countries to deal with any problems which might arise in this field.
Detailed discussions were held in the early part of 1959 regarding the United States oil restrictions. The voluntary controls which applied to oil in the early months of 1959 were replaced by a mandatory import control system. Strong representations were made to the United States government on this matter

and as a result of these discussions Canadian oil was freed from these import restrictions by a presidential proclamation of April, 1959.
No satisfactory solutions were found with regard to the restrictions imposed by the United States in October, 1958 on imports of lead and zinc. These restrictions constituted a serious impairment of United States trade agreement obligations to Canada and their continued application is a matter of real concern. The Canadian government has continued to press strongly the United States on this serious difficulty affecting trade relations between the two countries. A further investigation by the United States tariff commission into the domestic lead and zinc industry to see what additional United States restrictions, if any, needed to be imposed was undertaken but not completed during the year, and this investigation added to the uncertainties affecting trade in these items.
Apart from the problem of lead and zinc Canada's access to United States markets was unaffected by any major adverse developments. While there were a number of United States investigations to determine whether imports were causing or threatening injury to the United States industry, no adverse action was taken. Products involved included the following of interest to Canada, mink fur skins, calf leather, hardwood, plywood, and red fescue seed. A favourable development was the withdrawal on July 1 of escape clause action taken by the United States on alsike clover seed.
On February 16 and 17, 1960 the cabinet level joint Canada-United States committee on trade and economic affairs met again in Washington. The continuing expansion of economic activity in both countries was noted, as was the substantially improved economic and financial position of most other countries in the world. The committee discussed the prevalence of special restrictions on agricultural trade and emphasized the importance of pursuing policies which would encourage an expansion of trade. The committee discussed problems and developments which had arisen in trade between Canada and the United States in important items such as lead, zinc, crude oil, natural gas and uranium. Consideration was given to problems arising from rapid increases of imports into Canada and the United States in certain lines of low cost manufactured goods. Particular attention was paid to the situation arising from the Paris economic meetings of January 12-14 dealing with the establishment of the European economic community and the European free trade association and the need to find solutions to current trade problems in Europe
Business of the House
on a multilateral basis. There was an exchange of views on other matters including development aid to the less developed countries and proposals for the reconstitution of the organization for European economic co-operation.
Just before moving adjournment of the debate, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I will be able to complete my remarks tomorrow without too much trouble. I want to make it clear that Canada's trade is in a healthy condition. I want to make it clear that the government has been taking every measure open to it to stimulate Canadian trade. At the same time, I should like to pay my compliments to Canadian businessmen who have continued to press for an expansion of Canadian trade with all countries of the world.
May I move the adjournment of the debate?

FEDERAL BUILDING, DISRAELI, QUE.- REPAINTING TENDERS
speechtext:
1.	Were tenders called more than once In connection with the repainting of the federal building at Disraeli, Quebec?
2.	If so, by what method in each case?
3.	On what dates were tenders called and on what dates were they opened?
4.	What are the names of those who submitted tenders and what were the respective amounts of each tender in response to each call?
5.	To whom was the contract awarded?
Answer by: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
1.	Yes.
2.	Local public tender and invited tender call.
3.	(a) Local public tenders were called on November 17, 1959 and were returned to the tenderers unopened.
(b) Invited tenders were called on December 28, 1959 and were opened on January 15, 1960.
4.	(a) Local public tenders were received from:
Gilles Cote, Ste. Agathe de Black Lake; W. Grondin, Disraeli; J. L. Lafleur, Thetford Mines; Rene Lafleur, Thetford Mines.
(b) Invited tenders were received from: Raoul Allaire, Disraeli, $2,050; Robert Ger-vais, Disraeli, $2,150; Sylvio Fortin, Disraeli, $2,300.
5.	Contract awarded to Raoul Allaire.
